vulns.description: ### Summary  The client accepts and decompresses frames with the RSV1 bit set even when the `permessage-deflate` extension was not negotiated.  ### Impact  A client may unexpectedly decompress WebSocket frames when explicitly opted out. This could lead to additional CPU/memory consumption, but is unlikely to be a significant issue unless a zip bomb vulnerability or similar is also present.  ---  Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/47fb6ae354d4fa22048f4dbe7dbf82b625f0a2f6

### Summary  The HTTP parsers were vulnerable to a request smuggling attack relating to WebSocket upgrades.  ### Impact  If using the server-side component, it may be possible for an attacker to execute a request smuggling vulnerability using an edge case in the WebSocket upgrade procedure. AIOHTT is unaware of any public exploit code.  ---  Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/6ae358f0983c3f4d6f67692b2f8e65dc8e091c98

### Summary  An out-of-bounds heap read could occur in the C response parser while building an error message for a malformed response.  ### Impact  An attacker controlled server, or possibly an accidental response could trigger a DoS in the client.  ### Workaround  If unable to upgrade, the Python parser is unaffected and can be used with `AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS=1`.  ---  Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/49f65d54150397892f7bcc4aae887767d51c322d

### Summary  An out-of-bounds heap read could occur in the C response parser while building an error message for a malformed response.  ### Impact  An attacker controlled server, or possibly an accidental response could trigger a DoS in the client.  ### Workaround  If unable to upgrade, the Python parser is unaffected and can be used with `AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS=1`.  ---  Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/49f65d54150397892f7bcc4aae887767d51c322d

AIOHTT is unaware of any public exploit code.  ---  Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/6ae358f0983c3f4d6f67692b2f8e65dc8e091c98

This could lead to additional CPU/memory consumption, but is unlikely to be a significant issue unless a zip bomb vulnerability or similar is also present.  ---  Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/47fb6ae354d4fa22048f4dbe7dbf82b625f0a2f6

### Summary  The keepalive timeout was not used during the initial portion of a request.  ### Impact  An attacker could keep an idle connection open indefinitely before sending any data.  ### Workaround  Use a reverse proxy (as recommended for all production deployments) with sensible keepalive limits.

### Summary  Multiple cases were found where aiohttp could use excessive or unbounded memory, or excessive CPU consumption on attacker controlled requests.  ### Impact  An attacker could cause resource exhaustion through specially crafted requests.
### Summary  The Secure attribute was not being enforced for the shared cookie.  ### Impact  It may be possible to send a shared cookie marked Secure through an unencrypted request.

### Summary  The pure Python parser is vulnerable to an HTTP request smuggling attack.  ### Impact  If users are using the Python parser (`AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS`, or not a standard wheel installed), then an application may be vulnerable to a request smuggling attack.  ### Workaround  Switch to the default C parser.

### Summary  An attacker can exhaust file descriptors with specially crafted multipart requests.  ### Impact  If a handler uses `Request.post()`, it may be possible for an attacker to use an unlimited number of file descriptors, potentially resulting in resource exhaustion.

### Summary  A subdomain can remove the Host-Only flag from an existing cookie to a parent domain.  ### Impact  A user accessing untrusted subdomains could see their Host-Only protections stripped from cookies. Given most usecases won't reflect these cookies to a browser, the impact is limited.

### Summary  An overflow in Max-Age processing can skip closing a connection.  ### Impact  An attacker may be able to exhaust the connection pool temporarily, until garbage collection resolves the connections.

### Summary  An attacker sending an absolute-form request can spoof the scheme used.  ### Impact  If user code depends on the `Request.scheme` attribute for anything security related, an attacker may be able to circumvent this logic, tricking the application into thinking a connection is encrypted when it is not, or vice versa.  ### Workaround  A WAF rule to reject absolute-form requests (legitimate requests should only use this form for proxies).

vulns.description: ### Impact Services using internationalized (non-ASCII) domain names are potentially vulnerable to TLS connections made from AnyIO's `connect_tcp()` or directly via `TLSStream.wrap()` where the connection has (through other means) been hijacked and redirected to a malicious server. The attacker would obtain a legitimate certificate using the IDNA 2003 encoded version of the domain name and offer it to the connecting client, making the certificate validate properly on the client's end.  ### Patches The vulnerability will be patched in v4.14.2.  ### Workarounds Encode host names via the `idna` package prior to connecting.

### Impact AnyIO starts process-pool workers with stderr connected to a pipe but never drains that pipe. The worker redirects stdin and stdout to /dev/null to protect its protocol, but does not redirect stderr even though the documentation says all three standard streams are redirected. Worker code that writes enough attacker-influenced data to stderr can fill the pipe, block before returning the stdout protocol response, and wedge the awaiting process-pool call.  Anyone who runs untrusted or faulty code that writes too much to `stderr` is at risk.  ### Patches This vulnerability will be patched in v4.14.2.  ### Workarounds Closing `sys.stderr` in the target function should at least prevent the deadlock.

| | | |---|---| | Product | asyncssh (all versions through 2.23.0) | | Related | CVE-2019-6111 (same class in OpenSSH) | | Fix | AsyncSSH 2.23.1 | A malicious SSH server can write arbitrary files on the asyncssh SCP client's filesystem by sending filenames containing `../` traversal sequences. The SCP receive path does not currently sanitize server-provided filenames. By chaining directory traversals via the `D` (directory) action, an attacker can escape any target directory and overwrite `~/.bashrc`, `~/.ssh/rc`, or `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, achieving code execution. This is the same vulnerability class as CVE-2019-6111. The mitigation applied in OpenSSH does not appear to have been adopted in asyncssh. --- **Steps to exploit:** **Step 1 - Normal usage:** Application calls `await asyncssh.scp((conn, 'file'), '/home/user/downloads/')`. This is the standard, documented API. **Step 2 - SCP protocol:** asyncssh opens an SSH exec channel, runs `scp -f file`. The server controls the filename field: ``` C0644 100 ../pwned.txt (simple traversal) D0755 0 .. (traverse up, repeat as needed) C0644 47 .bashrc (write payload) E ``` **Step 3 - `_parse_cd_args`** (`scp.py:134-142`) returns the filename verbatim: ```python def _parse_cd_args(args: bytes) -> Tuple[int, int, bytes]: permissions, size, name = args.split(None, 2) return int(permissions, 8), int(size), name # no sanitization ``` The returned `name` is not passed through `basename()` and is not checked for `..` or `/` components. **Step 4 - `_recv_files`** (`scp.py:706-713`) joins the unsanitized name: ```python new_dstpath = posixpath.join(dstpath, name) ``` With `dstpath=b'/home/user/downloads/subdir'` and `name=b'../pwned.txt'`, this resolves to `/home/user/downloads/pwned.txt`, outside the target. **Step 5 - File write:** `_recv_file` opens the traversed path via `self._fs.open(dstpath, 'wb')` and writes attacker-controlled content. The resolved path is not checked against the target directory boundary. **Step 6 - RCE chains:** | Target | Execution trigger | Reliability | |---|---|---| | `~/.bashrc` | Next terminal open | High | | `~/.profile` | Next login | High | | `~/.ssh/rc` | Next SSH connection (requires sshd) | High | | `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` | Attacker logs in with `command=` | Medium | --- **Reproduction:** Link to reproduction script: [path_traversal_poc.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28160665/path_traversal_poc.zip) ```bash docker build -t asyncssh-scp-traversal -f Dockerfile . docker run --rm asyncssh-scp-traversal ``` The attached `poc_scp_traversal.py` starts a malicious SSH server in-process using asyncssh's own API, then downloads from it via `asyncssh.scp()`. *Expected Output:*

## Summary  A malicious SSH server can wedge an AsyncSSH **client**, and an authenticated client can wedge an AsyncSSH **server**, by sending a channel `maximum packet size` of `0` in `SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN_CONFIRMATION` (server→client) or `SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN` (client→server). AsyncSSH stores the peer-supplied value verbatim with no lower-bound check; the first time channel data is written, `SSHChannel._flush_send_buf` enters a **synchronous infinite loop** that cannot be interrupted by `asyncio.wait_for` or any timeout. The loop body has no `await`, so it blocks the entire asyncio event loop — for a server, one malicious authenticated channel freezes **all** current and future connections.  RFC 4254 §5.1 leaves receiver behavior for a peer-reported "maximum packet size = 0" undefined, so the value must be rejected rather than stored.  ## Root cause  `asyncssh/channel.py`:  ```python # process_open (server side)        -- line 465 self._send_pktsize = send_pktsize    # peer value, no >= 1 check  # process_open_confirmation (client) -- line 528 self._send_pktsize = send_pktsize    # peer value, no >= 1 check  # _flush_send_buf                    -- lines 305-320 while self._send_buf and self._send_window:     pktsize = min(self._send_window, self._send_pktsize)  # 0 when peer sends 0     buf, datatype = self._send_buf[0]     if len(buf) > pktsize:          # True for any buffered data         data = buf[:pktsize]        # empty (b'')         del buf[:pktsize]           # no-op     ...     self._send_window -= len(data)  # -= 0, unchanged ```  With `_send_pktsize == 0`, `pktsize` is `0`, so `buf[:0]` is empty, `del buf[:0]` is a no-op, and `_send_window` is never decremented — the `while` condition is permanently true, and with no `await` in the body the event loop is blocked.  ## Impact  - **Client vector (primary):** a malicious SSH server replies to the client's   channel open with `maximum packet size = 0`; the client wedges on its first   channel write. The attacker is the server, so it needs no valid credentials. - **Server vector:** an authenticated client opens a channel with   `maximum packet size = 0`; any server-side channel write wedges the AsyncSSH   server's event loop, freezing **every** current and future connection. A   single low-privilege account can take the whole server down.  Both vectors are a single SSH message, deterministic, and cause total availability loss for the affected process.  ## Affected versions  <= 2.23.1 (latest release, 2026-06-06); also present on `master` (channel.py:465/528 unguarded). Verified end-to-end on 2.23.1.  ## Verification  The maintainer's proposed fix (reject `send_pktsize == 0` in `connection.py` `_process_channel_open` / `_process_channel_open_confirmation`) was applied to 2.23.1 and re-tested end-to-end over TCP:  - **Unpatched:** malicious server (paramiko forcing `max_packet_size=0` in   OPEN_CONFIRMATION) + real asyncssh client → client event loop wedges. - **Patched:** the guard fires inside `_process_channel_open_confirmation`, the   malicious value is rejected, the connection closes cleanly   (`ChannelOpenError: SSH connection closed`), and the client does **not** wedge.  The maintainer (Ron Frederick) independently confirmed the freeze and noted that **even shutting the server down does not break clients out of the loop**.  Reproducers available: a focused harness driving the real `SSHChannel._flush_send_buf` with `_send_pktsize=0`, and an end-to-end `malicious_server.py` (paramiko) + `client.py` (real asyncssh) pair. The end-to-end client repro uses `asyncio.new_event_loop()` (not `get_event_loop()`) for Python 3.14 compatibility.  ## Suggested fix (maintainer's approach)  In `connection.py`, after each `send_pktsize = packet.get_uint32()` in `_process_channel_open` and `_process_channel_open_confirmation`:  ```python if send_pktsize == 0:     raise ProtocolError('Invalid maximum packet size') ```  ## CVSS  `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` (6.5 Medium). An earlier draft quoted 7.5 High ("100% CPU"); the synchronous loop burns ~100% of one core's worth of CPU but, being single-threaded, the OS scheduler spreads it across cores, so the real impact is event-loop / connection freeze, not machine-wide CPU exhaustion.  ## References  - RFC 4254 §5.1 (channel "maximum packet size"; behavior for 0 is undefined). - The same `maximum packet size = 0` send-loop wedge was confirmed in several   other independent SSH implementations (different languages/runtimes) and   reported to each maintainer separately.  ## Credits  Reported by zhangph (afldl), 2026-06-20. ```

### Summary  The GitHub Action bundled with Black can read the version from `tool.black.required-version` if `use_pyproject` is set to True. This version is not validated and therefore can be used to execute untrusted code in the context of a victim's repository.  ### Details  This is similar to the previous CVE-2026-31900. The value in `tool.black.required-version` is accepted as the version to be installed by the action without validation.  ### Proof of concept  Reproduction requires a victim to use Black's GitHub Action with `use_pyproject: true`. The attacker would then issue a PR to the victim's repository with `pyproject.toml` edited so that Black points to a malicious repository.  ### Impact  This is a remote code execution vulnerability impacting users using the GitHub Action bundled with psf/black and using the `use_pyproject: true` setting.

CVE-2026-111497 ("Node2Shell") is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) in Google's Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c). DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() returns an ambiguous value for an invalid block switch, and the fast decode path discards it (CWE-252, unchecked return value), so a crafted Brotli stream makes the decoder continue on corrupted state and write past the ring buffer. Upstream rates it CVSS 4.0 9.2 and classifies the impact as potential remote code execution.  The vulnerability is in Google's C library, not in Node.js specifically. The PyPI `Brotli` package is Google's CPython binding and compiles the same c/dec/decode.c that has the original vulnerability. All `Brotli` releases up to and including 1.2.0 ship the vulnerable decoder; 1.2.1 contains the upstream fix (commit 0ed4268a) and differs from 1.2.0 only in that fix plus a version bump.  The decoder is reached whenever untrusted Brotli data is decompressed. With `brotlicffi` installed, common HTTP clients decode Brotli responses automatically (urllib3/requests, httpx with the brotli extra, aiohttp) and services that accept `Content-Encoding: br` request bodies decode inbound data, so the flaw is reachable from attacker-controlled input.

Certifi versions before 2026.10.18 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root certificate in their bundled CA store. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to this root have compromised private keys and the CA has revoked them.   An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname. If the attacker is also on-path, they can intercept or modify TLS traffic from clients that trust the certifi bundle. Examples include `requests`, `urllib3` and `pip`, and the Python.org macOS installer.  Certifi 2026.10.18 removed all emSign roots from the bundle. Certifi 2026.10.19 restored the emSign roots that are not affected. Upgrade to 2026.10.19 or later, and rebuild container images that vendor certifi.

vulns.description: ### Summary  `pkcs7_decrypt_der`, `pkcs7_decrypt_pem`, and `pkcs7_decrypt_smime` reported the outcome of decrypting a `RecipientInfo`'s `encryptedKey` in several distinguishable ways, one of which disclosed the exact length recovered from the RSA operation. The same distinction was also observable by timing. An application that decrypts attacker-supplied `EnvelopedData` and reflects the outcome gives the attacker a Bleichenbacher oracle against the content-encryption key.  Introduced in 44.0.0. Fixed in 50.0.0.  ### Details  Decryption ran as: RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 decrypt of `encryptedKey` → build an AES cipher from the result → AES-CBC decrypt and PKCS#7 unpad. Each stage failed differently, with no RFC 3218 mitigation:  1. invalid RSA padding → `Decryption failed` 2. valid padding, bad key length → `Invalid key size (N) for AES.`, disclosing `N` 3. correct length, wrong key → `Invalid padding bytes.` 4. the real key → plaintext  Case 1 is reachable only where the linked library lacks implicit rejection: OpenSSL 3.0 and 3.1, LibreSSL, and BoringSSL. On OpenSSL 3.2+, used in our wheels, invalid padding instead returns a synthetic plaintext of pseudorandom length, so the error channel does not distinguish conforming ciphertexts.  Exploitation requires a service that auto-decrypts untrusted `EnvelopedData` matching the victim certificate and answers adaptively at high volume, such as an S/MIME gateway or mail filter.  ### Fix  Per RFC 3218, the content-encryption algorithm is now resolved before the private key is used, so the expected key length is known in advance. If the RSA decryption fails or recovers a key of the wrong length, a random key of the expected length is substituted and decryption continues down an identical path. All failures now report identically and perform the same work.  ### Not addressed by this fix  `EnvelopedData` does not authenticate its content. Tampering with `encryptedContent` alone yields a CBC padding oracle that recovers plaintext at roughly 256 queries per byte, without recovering any key, on every backend. This is a property of PKCS#7 rather than of this implementation, cannot be fixed in the library, and is now documented.  ### Credit  Reported by @X1AOxiang.

`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) hand SQLite a name they do not control. On Linux the lock validates its database through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file). It then connects SQLite to `/proc/self/fd/<n>`, a Linux path that names the process's own open file `n`. SQLite turns that path back into a plain path and reopens it by name, following symlinks (a symlink is a file that points at another path). On every POSIX route SQLite also acts on `-journal`, `-wal` and `-shm` files it finds beside that name. Those are SQLite's side files: the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write), the write-ahead log or WAL (changes kept outside the main file), and the shared-memory index for the WAL.  Another local user who can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can turn this against the user running the lock (below: the lock user). Such a directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). That other user can make the lock user's ordinary `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` write bytes of the other user's choosing into the lock user's own files. The same position lets the other user make that call create or unlink files of the lock user, admit a reader beside a writer, or kill the holder. All of this runs with the lock user's privileges. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp` a planted `-wal` file makes every acquire fail. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 (the `/proc/self/fd` redirect since 4.0.9, the side-file variants since 3.20.4).  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J` [high, CWE-363]: ReadWriteLock: SQLite still follows planted symlinks, overwriting files.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H` scores 7.1 (High).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): the planted-journal variant needs no race, and the redirect won 77 of 77 attempts. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user writes bytes of their choosing into files of the lock user and unlinks files of their choosing. `A:H` (high availability impact): the other user makes every acquire fail or kills the lock holder. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges.  Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, a cross-user effect that exists only when another user can change names in the lock database's directory. The review notes that the 77/77 inotify result (inotify is a Linux interface that reports file events) is stronger evidence than a theoretical TOCTOU (a time-of-check to time-of-use race). The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism and narrows it to that precondition.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other party is a different local account that can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database. That is a `0777` directory or a group-writable one (including a setgid `2775` project directory shared with that account), in each case without the sticky bit. The lock user's lock must be able to open the database read-write, so a database the other user creates is `0666`. filelock itself creates the database `0600`. - Sticky directories (`/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, any `1777` directory) narrow the finding rather than exclude it. The redirect and the journal replay do not reach a database the lock user owns there (tested with `fs.protected_regular=2`). What remains is a planted non-empty `<db>-wal` (any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) that the lock user cannot unlink. It makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. A hard link (a second name for the same file) to a file of the lock user at the lock path also remains, if `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. - Two kernel settings matter. `fs.protected_regular` (1 or 2 is the systemd default on most distributions; the kernel's own default is 0) keeps a user from opening a file another user owns in a sticky world-writable directory. Where it is 0, the other user can own the database in `/tmp`, and SQLite follows a planted symlink itself (not tested). `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (most distributions; kernel default 0) blocks a hard link of a lock user's file onto the lock path. Neither setting affects a non-sticky shared directory. - Platform and route. The `/proc/self/fd` redirect is Linux with `/proc` mounted, 4.0.9 and later. The side-file variants (`-journal`, `-wal`, `-shm`) exist on every POSIX route. On the hard-link route (macOS since 4.1.1 for every connection, Linux without `/proc`) they need the link-directory swap described under "Mechanism", so a non-sticky parent. Neither the scanner nor the review executed on macOS; the statement rests on the platform branch and the identical code after it. Windows does not take this path. - Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename an entry in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_connect_through_descriptor` builds `/proc/self/fd/<n>` and hands it to `sqlite3.connect`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L982-L1001). The assumption is the [comment at line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), "Descriptor paths reopen the validated inode" (an inode is the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name). SQLite first reads the file it opened at [`PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, line 816](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L816). The check in [`_raise_if_database_replaced` at line 836](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L836) runs only after `BEGIN`. Both [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) inspect the descriptor, not the file SQLite is on. The one-level hard link of the macOS route is [`_link_beside`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1014-L1029).  ## Introduced  The `/proc/self/fd` redirect came with `4d45e83` ("Merge commit from fork", the fix for GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56), first released in **4.0.9** (verified: `git tag --contains 4d45e83` gives 4.0.9); 4.0.8 does not have it. The side-file variants are older. They reproduce on `cfd4446` ("feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock (#399)"), first released in **3.20.4** (verified), which passed the lock path straight to `sqlite3.connect`.  ## Mechanism  On Linux the lock opens the database with `O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK`. It checks through the descriptor that the file is a regular file and not a WAL database. It then calls `sqlite3.connect("/proc/self/fd/<n>")` and expects SQLite to reopen the validated inode. SQLite does not open that name. It runs `readlink()` on it, which yields the path string the kernel reports for the descriptor at that moment, and opens that string by path, following every symlink. Without interference the trace shows `readlink("/proc/534/fd/3") = "/tmp/benign/app.lock.db"` and then a second `openat` of that path. The descriptor contributes only a string. Once the directory entry behind the descriptor is gone, the string is `<database> (deleted)`. A symlink with that exact name sends SQLite wherever its creator chose.  The other user prepares the directory before the lock user runs. They create a database `cache.lock.db` (`0666`, so the lock user's lock accepts it) with a second hard link `cache.lock.db.keep`, and the symlink `cache.lock.db (deleted) -> /tmp/victim-notes.txt`. The lock user's `os.open` raises an inotify `IN_OPEN` event. The other user unlinks `cache.lock.db` and links `cache.lock.db.keep` back under the same name. The lock user's descriptor still refers to the unlinked entry, so `/proc/self/fd/3` now reads `/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)`. `sqlite3.connect` resolves it, follows the symlink and opens the target `O_RDWR|O_CREAT`. None of filelock's checks look at that file. `_open_lock_database` and `_raise_if_wal` inspect descriptor 3. `_raise_if_database_replaced` compares an `lstat` of the lock path with the descriptor's `(st_dev, st_ino)`, which passes because the other user linked the same inode back, and it runs only after `BEGIN`.  The damage comes from the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`. SQLite finds `<target>-journal`, treats it as the rollback journal of an interrupted transaction, and copies its page records into the target before it checks whether the target is a database at all. The journal header supplies the page size and the page count SQLite resizes the file to. Whoever wrote the journal computed the per-page checksum. The content from offset 0 and the final length are therefore the other user's. Strace of the lock user's process (SQLite 3.40.1):  ``` openat("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NONBLOCK|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0600) = 3 readlink("/proc/3819/fd/3", "/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)", 4096) = 41 readlink("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)", "/tmp/victim-notes.txt", 4096) = 21 openat("/tmp/victim-notes.txt", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0644) = 4 openat("/tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal", O_RDWR|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC) = 5 pread64(5, "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE "..., 4096, 516) = 4096 pwrite64(4, "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE "..., 4096, 0) = 4096 unlink("/tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal") = -1 EPERM            -> "disk I/O error" ```  The redirect itself needs no journal. The constructor's validation connection already makes SQLite open the target with `O_CREAT`. With the symlink pointing at a missing path in the lock user's home, constructing the lock created that file (empty, `0644`, owned by the lock user) and raised nothing. With the symlink pointing at a `0600` WAL-mode SQLite database of the lock user, `write_lock()` returned without error and the database's header bytes 18 and 19 changed from `2 2` to `1 1`. The pragma converted the lock user's database out of WAL mode, and the redirected acquire held its SQLite lock on that database rather than on the lock database.  **Side-file names beside the database.** Two comments record the belief that SQLite names its side files after the descriptor path ([line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), [line 1095](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1095)). The path is not synthetic to SQLite. It derives `<database>-journal`, `<database>-wal` and `<database>-shm` from the resolved real path in the shared directory. `journal_mode=MEMORY` governs only journals SQLite would write, not ones it finds. These variants need no redirect.  *A hot `-journal` makes the lock user unlink a file the journal names; no race.* The other user unlinks the lock user's empty `lock.db`, puts a one-page SQLite database (`0666`) in its place, and writes a 46-byte `lock.db-journal`: a path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. SQLite treats a journal beside a non-empty database as hot (left by an interrupted transaction). The tail names a "super-journal", and recovery ends by unlinking that file. The lock user's next `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` returns without error and the named file is gone (`unlink("/home/victim/private/notes.txt") = 0`, from a `0700` directory of the lock user). The named file must be a non-empty regular file the lock user can read and unlink. A FIFO planted as `lock.db-journal` instead blocks `read_lock(timeout=2)` in SQLite's `open()` of the journal (still blocked when killed after 10 s).  *A re-planted `-wal` puts the holder in WAL mode past `_raise_if_wal`.* `_raise_if_wal` checks header bytes 18 and 19. Whenever a connection takes its first lock, SQLite stats `<db>-wal`, and if that file and the database are both non-empty it opens the WAL whatever the header says. The pragma at line 816 converts such a database and unlinks `-wal` and `-shm`. The `BEGIN` at line 833 is a separate statement that starts unlocked and stats `<db>-wal` again. Re-creating the 32-byte `-wal` in that gap landed on the first attempt in 20 of 20 runs on a 2-CPU machine.  The lock user's `with lock.write_lock():` then holds the `-shm` byte-120 WAL write lock and only SHARED on the database. Once the other user removes the `-wal`, a second process of the lock user gets `read_lock(timeout=1)` granted while the writer is inside its block, with no exception on either side. SQLite also creates `<db>-shm` with the database's permission bits (`0666`) and keeps it mapped into memory. After the other user truncates it, the writer dies with `SIGBUS` (the signal for touching a mapped file region that no longer exists) in `connection.rollback()` during `release()`.  *A `-wal` in a sticky directory makes every acquire raise; no race, no access to the database.* Beside the lock user's own empty `0600` database, a non-empty `<db>-wal` (one byte, any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) is a leftover SQLite tries to delete. In a `1777` directory the lock user cannot unlink another user's file (`unlink(...) = -1 EPERM`), so the pragma fails with `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`. The code in [`_do_acquire_inner`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L763) translates only "database is locked" into `Timeout`. `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` therefore leaves every `acquire_read()` / `acquire_write()` (and the async variants) within milliseconds, whatever `timeout` or `blocking` says, until the file's owner or root removes it.  *Further effects observed at this commit in a non-sticky directory.* A `0755` script owned by the lock user, renamed to the lock path with a one-record journal beside it, ends up holding the other user's bytes (the acquire raises `file is not a database`). A hard link to the lock user's `0600` `~/.profile` at the lock path does the same in a sticky `/tmp` when `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. When the locking process runs as root, SQLite runs `fchown` on a `-wal` or `-shm` it opens to match the owner of the database, so root's `0600` `service.env` renamed to `app.lock.db-wal` belonged to the other user after root's `read_lock()`.  A journal whose super-journal names the database itself makes SQLite open and close a second descriptor on the database, which drops the process's POSIX locks, so `acquire_read` returns with no lock held in `/proc/locks` and a writer in another process acquires (two journals in a row, one per statement; write locks are not affected). A one-byte `lock.db-wal` plus a `lock.db-shm` on which the other user holds two byte locks makes the acquire take 10 s regardless of `timeout` and raise `locking protocol`, or die with `SIGBUS` if the other user truncates the `-shm`.  **The hard-link route in a directory without the sticky bit.** None of the above occurs on the `_link_beside` branch (macOS, Linux without `/proc`). There SQLite's main file is `.filelock-…/lock.db` in the connecting user's `0700` directory. That protection holds only where no other user can rename the `.filelock-*` entry itself, because `0700` protects the contents, not the entry in the parent. `_link_beside` checks the link once and returns a pathname, and every later use is by that name.  With `/proc` hidden in a `0777` directory, the other user staged a directory holding a hard link `lock.db` to a one-page database and a hot `lock.db-journal`. They held `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE` on the database so the lock user's first statement waited in the busy handler (SQLite's retry loop for a locked database), renamed the lock user's `.filelock-*` directory aside, renamed the staged directory onto its name and rolled back. SQLite got SHARED, found the journal under the swapped name and unlinked the file it named. The lock user's process reported the lock held and exited 0. A polling variant without the write lock also won (in 40 trials the file was gone after 1 to 26 starts of the lock user's program). Under the sticky bit the rename fails with `EPERM`.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J`, quoted as received. The process writes bytes of the other user's choosing from offset 0 into any non-empty regular file the lock user can write, resized to a whole number of pages, provided the other user can create `<file>-journal` beside it (the lock user's own `0600` files in `/tmp` qualify). Without a journal the process creates an empty file at any path it may create, or converts a WAL-mode SQLite database of its own to rollback mode with no error. A journal beside a swapped-in database makes the process unlink one regular file of the other user's choosing per journal; the acquire succeeds and raises nothing. A process inside `write_lock()` stops excluding the lock user's other processes from `read_lock()`, and the holder can die from a `SIGBUS` that arrives in `release()`.  It is **not** reachable for a database the lock user owns in `/tmp` with `fs.protected_regular` 1 or 2. There only the planted `-wal` denial of service remains: every acquire raises an undocumented `sqlite3.OperationalError` that `Timeout` and `OSError` handlers do not catch. It is a bypass of the fix for GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56 (4.0.9), which refused the symlink at the database path but followed it at `<database> (deleted)`. Windows does not take this path.  ## Workarounds  - Keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share one `ReadWriteLock` database between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory. The lock creates its database `0600`, and leaving it that way keeps other accounts from supplying its content. - For a lock in a sticky directory keep `fs.protected_regular` at 1 or 2 and `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (distribution defaults). Treat a sudden `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` on every acquire as a foreign `<db>-wal` beside the database that the file's owner or root has to remove.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. On Windows, `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) connect SQLite to the lock database by its path, in every directory. SQLite derives three side files from that path: `<database>-journal`, the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write); `<database>-wal`, the write-ahead log (changes kept outside the main file); and `<database>-shm`, the shared-memory index of the WAL. SQLite acts on whichever of these it finds beside the database before the lock runs any statement. Another local account that can create files in the database's directory, but not delete files of other accounts there, places such a side file beside the database and denies everyone `DELETE` on it, which a file's creator may do. `C:\Windows\Temp` (the temporary directory of services, granting `BUILTIN\Users` create but not delete) and `C:\Users\Public` are such directories.  With a `-wal` in place, every `read_lock()` and `write_lock()` of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) raises `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` at once, whatever `timeout` says, until that account removes its file; the lock user cannot. With a `-journal` beside a lock database that holds a table, SQLite replays the journal and deletes the file the journal names, a file of the lock user, and the acquire reports success. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the POSIX form of the defect, GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8, whose text says "Windows does not take this path" (review round 4, finding F2 of set D). It is not among the findings of the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 3.3 (Low).**  `AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): create one file beside the database and set its ACL (access control list); no race, and the other account can place the file days earlier. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account that can create files in the directory is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other account learns nothing. `I:N` (no integrity impact in the scored variant): see the scoring note. `A:L` (partial availability impact): every acquire fails with an exception that `Timeout` handlers do not catch, until the other account removes its file; no crash, and the lock's own data is not changed. The lower-reading rule of this advisory set scores the variant that reaches every `ReadWriteLock` on Windows in such a directory, 3.3, and describes the deletion variant under Mechanism. Classification from the review: **security** (another account), availability for the scored variant.  ## Scope and preconditions  - Platform and classes: Windows only. `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock`, both of which connect through `_connect`. On Linux and macOS the lock takes other routes, covered by GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8. - Directory: one where another account can create files but cannot delete the lock user's. `C:\Windows\Temp` carries `BUILTIN\Users:(CI)(S,WD,AD,X)` (create file and create subdirectory, no delete child); `C:\Users\Public` and any directory with such an entry qualify. A directory only the lock user can write, such as `%LOCALAPPDATA%` or the per-user temporary directory, is not affected. - The other account creates `<database>-wal`, grants everyone modify and denies everyone `DELETE` on it. A file's creator may set both. The lock user can open and read the file but not delete it. - Deletion variant: the lock database holds at least one table (filelock creates an empty database, and the review's reproducer has the lock account create the table), and the other account's `<database>-journal` grants the lock account modify rights. The journal's tail names a file the lock user can delete. - What the lock user sees: `write_lock(timeout=1)` raised `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` with the undeletable `-wal` in place; with the writable journal the acquire succeeded and the named file was gone; with an undeletable journal every acquire raised `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file`. - The documentation at the scanned commit states "the lock directory must not be writable by untrusted users" for `WindowsFileLock`, in its symlink paragraph; the `ReadWriteLock` documentation names no directory requirement on Windows.  ## Affected code  Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [Windows branch of `_connect`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L951-L965) checks the database through a handle and then calls `sqlite3.connect(database, ...)` with the path. The reproducer ran against the head of PR #834 at `1f9e415`, whose Windows branch of `_connect` is the same code as at `b831496b0273`.  ## Mechanism  `_connect` on Windows opens the database with `_open_non_reparse_fd`, checks through that handle that the file is a regular file, not a reparse point, and that its header does not declare WAL mode, and keeps the handle open while `sqlite3.connect(database)` opens the same name. The check covers the database, not the names beside it. On the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, SQLite takes its first lock on the database and looks for `<database>-wal`. A non-empty `-wal` beside a database that is not in WAL mode is a leftover SQLite deletes. The other account's file denies `DELETE`, so the pragma raises `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`, which reaches the caller as `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. `_do_acquire_inner` converts only "database is locked" into `Timeout`, so `acquire_read()`, `acquire_write()` and the async forms raise at once, on every call, until the file is gone. The lock user has no right to delete it.  The journal variant needs a database with content. Beside a non-empty database SQLite treats a `<database>-journal` with a valid header as hot (left by an interrupted write) and replays it before the first statement runs. The review's journal is 46 bytes: a file path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. That tail names a super-journal, and recovery ends by deleting the file it names. The lock user's `write_lock()` therefore deletes one file the other account chose, provided the lock user can delete it, and returns without error. SQLite opens a hot journal for writing, so the other account's journal must grant the lock account modify rights; a read-only journal makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file` instead. The scanner and the maintainers measured the same side-file effects on Linux for GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8.  ## Impact  In a directory such as `C:\Windows\Temp`, another local account turns every `read_lock()` and `write_lock()` on a `ReadWriteLock` database into an immediate `sqlite3.OperationalError`, for as long as its file stays. Callers that handle `Timeout` or `OSError` do not catch it, and the lock user cannot remove the file. With a lock database that holds a table and a journal the lock user can write, the lock user's process deletes one file of the other account's choosing, among the files the lock user may delete, and the acquire reports success. The lock's own database is not changed, nothing is read, and mutual exclusion between processes that acquire the lock holds.  ## Workarounds  - Keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory other accounts cannot create files in: `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, the per-user temporary directory (`%TEMP%` of a user session), or a directory with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted. `C:\Windows\Temp` and `C:\Users\Public` do not qualify. - Treat `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` on every acquire as a foreign `<database>-wal` beside the database, which only its creator or an administrator can remove.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.  Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, finding F4); it is not among the scanner's findings.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 2.5 (Low).**  `AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): Windows grants a Level 1 or batch oplock only to the sole open handle on a file, so the marker must have no holder handle when the other account asks. That account cannot bring this about; it waits for a holder that died, closed its descriptor, or left a marker past its `lifetime`. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account with read access to the marker through the directory's inherited ACL (access control list). `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` and `I:N`: that account can read the marker's content (process id and host name) anyway, and mutual exclusion holds. `A:L` (partial availability impact): one thread, or the event loop with `run_in_executor=False`, waits until the holder answers; 10 s per attempt in the two-account runs, no crash. Metrics in doubt take the lower reading.  Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on an unheld marker that another account can open.  ## Scope and preconditions  - Platform and classes: Windows only. `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, `AsyncSoftFileLock` and the other async soft locks, and `FileLock` after its `ENOSYS` fallback to a soft lock. `WindowsFileLock` opens its lock file on a separate code path that this advisory does not cover. - Marker access: the soft locks create the marker with `os.open`, which on Windows applies no more of `mode` than the read-only attribute (GHSA-8mx5-7m5m-r77g). The marker carries the lock directory's inheritable entries. Another account that those entries grant read access to new files can open the marker with a read handle that shares read, write and delete. - Unheld marker: no handle may be open on the marker when the other account requests the oplock. That is a holder that died and left its marker, a holder that closed its descriptor, or a marker whose `lifetime` has passed. While the holder keeps its handle, the request fails. - Holder behavior: the other account requests the oplock through an overlapped `DeviceIoControl` and never acknowledges the break. Windows cancels a thread's pending request when the thread exits, so the holder thread stays alive. A same-account process that answers slowly, such as an indexer, has the same effect for its answer time. - What the lock user sees: `SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1)` returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s with the second account's handle. In the same-account probe `os.open` with `O_RDONLY` was still running after 15 s and returned once the holder closed. The retry loop consults `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` between attempts only. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the event loop waits. - Stale break: `break_lock_file` renames and unlinks by path. Both calls wait in the same way, so a stale marker under such an oplock stays, and no process acquires the lock until the holder closes. - Not affected: mutual exclusion, and the lock reads, writes and deletes no file other than the marker.  ## Affected code  Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [`os.open` in `_read_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L323) ([function](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L312-L335)), called from [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) on every attempt that finds a marker, and from [`_unprobeable_holder`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L137), [`pid`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L164) and [`is_lock_held_by_us`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L179). On an existing marker that fails with `EEXIST` (or `EACCES` on Windows) at once; the same-account probe shows the failed exclusive create returning at once under an oplock too. `_acquire` then calls `_try_break_stale_lock`, which calls `_read_lock_file`: `os.lstat`, then `os.open(path, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`. On Windows `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK` do not exist (the code reads them with `getattr(os, ..., 0)`), and `os.open` calls `CreateFileW`. When another handle holds a Level 1 or batch oplock on the file, that call sends the holder a break request and returns only when the holder acknowledges it or closes its handle. `_check_give_up` tests the deadline after the attempt returns, so the wait overruns `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` by its length. Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.  A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. ### Summary  `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` resolve the lock path with `pathlib.Path.resolve()` and pass it to `sqlite3.connect()` without refusing a symlink. A local user who can create names in the lock's directory, such as `/tmp` or a shared cache, can plant a symlink at the lock path and make the victim's process create, lock, or write the file it points to, or break mutual exclusion between the victim's own processes.  ### Details  `ReadWriteLock.__init__` stores `pathlib.Path(lock_file).resolve()`, which follows a final symlink, and every connection opens that path through `sqlite3.connect()` with no `O_NOFOLLOW` or regular-file check. SQLite's own VFS also resolves the final symlink in user space, so `fs.protected_symlinks` and the sticky bit do not help: the kernel never sees a symlink to refuse. The other lock classes do not follow a final symlink: `FileLock` opens with `O_NOFOLLOW`, and `SoftReadWriteLock` coordinates through `<path>.rw/`.  ### Proof of concept  On Linux, with the victim and attacker as different users and `/shared` mode 1777 with `fs.protected_symlinks=1`:  1. The attacker runs `ln -s /home/victim/private/pwned.flag /shared/app.rwlock.db`. 2. The victim constructs `ReadWriteLock("/shared/app.rwlock.db")`. A plain `os.open(..., O_NOFOLLOW)` on the same path fails, but the lock creates `/home/victim/private/pwned.flag`, owned by the victim, inside a directory the attacker cannot write. 3. With `/shared/cache.rwlock.db -> /shared/a.db`, one victim process holds the write lock. The attacker repoints the link to `/shared/b.db`, and a second victim process acquires the write lock while the first still holds it.  The same behavior reproduces on macOS, on Windows 11, and through `AsyncReadWriteLock`.  ### Impact  A local attacker with write access to the lock directory can make the victim create empty files it owns at paths the attacker cannot write, make the victim hold a SQLite lock on another application's database so that application gets `database is locked`, and give two victim processes the write lock at once, letting them corrupt the resource the lock protects.  ### Workarounds  Keep `ReadWriteLock` paths in directories that only trusted users can write.

filelock on Windows ignores the `mode` argument. `FileLock(path, mode=0o600)` creates the same file as `FileLock(path)`: one with no security descriptor of its own (the Windows record that says who may access a file). Its access list, or ACL, is whatever the lock directory hands down to new files. filelock creates the `ReadWriteLock` database, which it asks to be `0o600`, the same way. In a directory whose inheritable ACL grants other local accounts access to new files, those accounts can open the lock file or database. They can take the byte-range lock (a lock on a span of bytes in a file) once the owner releases it and keep the owner's later `acquire()` calls waiting or timing out. They can read holder metadata an `on_acquired` hook left in a `preserve_lock_file=True` file. Where the directory hands down modify access, they can write to both files.  `lock.mode` still reports `0o600`. The documentation neither promises an ACL on Windows nor says that Windows drops the mode. On Unix the same mode keeps other accounts out. Mutual exclusion between processes that follow the protocol holds on either platform. Affected versions are filelock 3.10.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows.  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private. Finding covered by this advisory:  - `ANT-2026-0KEO0DDO` [medium, CWE-732]: WindowsFileLock ignores mode; 0o600 lock files inherit the directory ACL.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L` scores 5.3 (Medium).**  `AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): no race. `C:L` (partial confidentiality impact): the lock file (holder metadata) and the lock database are readable where `0o600` was meant to keep them private. `I:L` (partial integrity impact): in the directory layout the maintainers tested, the other account can also write both files, which lets it corrupt the lock's own state but nothing the lock protects. `A:L` (partial availability impact): the other account can hold the byte-range lock and make the owner wait or time out. `S:U` (scope unchanged).  Classification from the review: **Windows permission failure with security impact only where callers rely on `mode=0o600` across accounts**. The review had marked it an unconfirmed Windows claim, since the scanner traced stand-in Win32 calls on Linux. The maintainers have since confirmed it on Windows with two local accounts (see Evidence). The scanner rated this medium; the maintainers keep medium.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The affected classes are `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Windows (`WindowsFileLock`), and the SQLite database of `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock`. Both go through `_open_non_reparse_fd`. The soft locks create their markers with `os.open`, which also keeps only a read-only bit of the mode on Windows; the scanner did not examine them further. - The directory is one that other local accounts cannot write, which the documentation already requires on Windows, but whose inheritable entries grant them read (or modify) access to new files. Examples are a service's data directory readable by `Users`, or any directory with `(OI)(CI)` entries (entries that new files and sub-directories inherit) for another account. A directory whose ACL already excludes other accounts, such as one inside a user profile, hides the problem. - The other account must open the file. According to the `LockFileEx` documentation, read access is enough to take the byte-range lock, so it can hold the lock whenever the owner does not. The lock file exists while the owner holds the lock, and stays after release with `preserve_lock_file=True`. The `ReadWriteLock` database is not unlinked at any point. - Unix is not affected, because `UnixFileLock` creates the file with the mode and repeats it with `fchmod`. Mutual exclusion between cooperating processes is not affected.  ## Affected code  Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_open_non_reparse_fd` reduces the mode to one `read_only` bit](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_windows.py#L252-L253). That bit is false for every accepted mode, because [`_check_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L526) rejects any mode without owner read and write, and an unset mode becomes `0o666`. In [`_nt_open`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_windows.py#L283-L310) the `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES.SecurityDescriptor` field stays unassigned, and `read_only` only chooses `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY`. [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1086) passes `0o600` through the same function on Windows.  ## Introduced  [d0061e4](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d0061e4643df) "added multiuser support and associated tests" ([#192](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/192), 2023-03-15), first tag 3.10.0 (verified), added the `mode` parameter and on Windows handed it to `os.open`, which applies only the read-only attribute. The Windows backend has applied no more of the mode than that at any version, so this is a long-standing gap rather than a regression.  ## Mechanism  `_open_non_reparse_fd(path, mode)` computes `read_only = not mode & _OWNER_WRITE` and calls `_nt_open(path, read_only=read_only)`. `_nt_open` fills an `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES` with the NT path and `OBJ_CASE_INSENSITIVE` and leaves `SecurityDescriptor` NULL. It then calls `NtCreateFile` with `FILE_OPEN_IF` and `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL` (or `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY` when `read_only`, which no accepted mode produces). Nothing consults the group and other bits. Per the `NtCreateFile` and `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES` documentation, a NULL descriptor gives the new file default security, which on NTFS is the set of inheritable entries of the parent directory. A lock file created with `mode=0o600` in a directory that hands down read access to `Users` is therefore readable by `Users`.  Nothing tells the caller. The constructor validates the mode, `lock.mode` returns `0o600`, and `has_explicit_mode` is `True`. `docs/concepts.rst` says "filelock creates the file with it" and that "`0o600` and `0o700` keep other UIDs out", with no Windows caveat. Only the `_open_non_reparse_fd` docstring and a comment in `_soft.py` record the limitation.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-0KEO0DDO`, quoted as received. `UnixFileLock`, the backend of `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Unix, empties whatever regular file it finds at the lock path once it holds the `flock` (a kernel lock on an open file). With an explicit `mode` it also chmods that file (sets its permission bits), whether or not this acquire created it. Another local user who can rename or hard-link one of the files of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) onto the lock path gets that file truncated by the lock user's next `acquire()`. A hard link is a second name for the same file. With a mode such as `0o666` the file, still owned by the lock user, also becomes readable and writable by that other user. The other user can then read and alter everything the lock user writes to it afterwards.  `O_NOFOLLOW`, the defence added for the symlink variant (CVE-2025-68146), does not see a renamed file or a hard link. The rename route needs the file's directory to be writable without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). The hard-link route into a sticky directory such as `/tmp` needs `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`, a Linux kernel setting. Affected versions are every filelock release up to and including 4.2.0 (the truncation is as old as the project; the chmod since 3.10.2).  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private. With a permissive explicit `mode` the other user can then write to it. If that file is one the lock user later executes or trusts, that is code execution as the lock user. `C:L` (partial confidentiality impact): the old content is gone before the other user can read anything, but what the lock user writes afterwards through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file) it still holds is readable. `A:N` (no availability impact). `S:U` (scope unchanged). That is the case on first use, after a reboot, after a `/tmp` cleaner, or after a release with the default `preserve_lock_file=False`, which unlinks the file. The scanner checked three ways at the scanned commit, with default kernel settings unless stated:   - rename inside a directory without the sticky bit (a group-writable project or cache directory, a root-created `0777` directory);   - rename from such a directory into a sticky one (`1777`) on the same filesystem. The sticky bit only protects entries that already exist, so the move succeeds while the lock path is free. Once the lock user's lock file exists there, the same move fails with `EPERM`;   - `link(2)` into a sticky directory. This needs a system that lets a user hard-link a file it cannot write, which on Linux means `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. Mainstream distributions set 1, which refuses the link. The scanner did not test macOS or the BSDs. - What the lock user loses: with the default `FileLock(path)` the lock truncates the file, which keeps its mode. With an explicit `mode` (a lock shared between users needs `0o666` or `0o660`, because `UnixFileLock` opens the file read-write), the lock also chmods the file to that mode. `_apply_explicit_mode` suppresses `PermissionError` only for files the lock user does not own. The lock user owns its own files, so the `fchmod` succeeds. - Trust boundary: the protection against another local user holds only when no other user can rename entries in the lock's directory or, for the rename-into-sticky route, in any directory on the same filesystem that holds a file of the lock user. With the lock user's file renamed to the lock path that fails with `FileExistsError`. The second `os.open(path, O_RDWR | O_NOFOLLOW)` succeeds, because the entry is a regular file the lock user owns, and returns `created = False`. `_acquire_native` passes `created` only to the `ENOSYS` branch. `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async variants and a `FileLock` that has fallen back to a soft lock on `ENOSYS` decide from the record inside the marker file whether its owner is gone. The marker is the file whose presence says a process holds the lock. They do not check who could have written that record.  A local user who can write the marker but cannot remove it rewrites the holder's record to name a dead PID (process id). That position arises with an explicit `mode` with group or other write bits, or the default mode under a lax umask (the process setting that strips permission bits from new files), in a sticky or otherwise non-removable directory. The sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it. The next contender running as the holder's account, or root, judges the lock stale, removes the live marker on that user's behalf and acquires it. Two processes then run the critical section together and neither gets an error. Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on another user being able to write the live marker. The scanner rated it high (CWE-345). The default mode under umask `022` is not affected.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other user can write the marker. The application passes a `mode` with group or other write bits, which `fchmod` applies as given since 4.1.0. `0o666` is a common choice for a lock shared between accounts, although a soft-lock contender of another account waits as well on a `0o644` marker, since contenders only read and rename. Or the application uses the default mode (`0o666` through the umask) under umask `002` in a directory whose group the other user belongs to, or under umask `000`. The default mode under umask `022` is not affected. - The other user cannot remove the marker itself: the directory is sticky, or the other user cannot write it at all (a `0755` directory owned by the lock's user gives the same overlap). In a non-sticky shared directory the other user can unlink the marker without filelock, and filelock adds nothing. - A contender that may rename the marker asks for the lock: another process of the holder's account (several workers of one user) or root. A contender of another unprivileged account cannot rename the marker in a sticky directory and times out. - The finding reaches every class that publishes a soft marker: `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async variants, and `FileLock(mode=0o666)` on a filesystem where `flock` (a kernel lock on an open file) fails with `ENOSYS`.  These protections against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it, which no file-based lock can defend against.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit b831496: the create mode in [`SoftFileLock._acquire`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L67-L71), the explicit-mode `fchmod` in [`_apply_explicit_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L100-L105), the trusting verdict in [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) and the [`owner_is_stale`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_identity.py#L64-L79) it relies on; the same call in [`MarkerSoftFileLock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_marker.py#L74-L81) and [`SoftFileLease`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_lease.py#L229-L256).  ## Introduced  The stale verdict that trusts the record came in with e35c3afac473 ("feat(soft): detect and break stale locks", #476, 2026-02-13), first released in 3.22.0. The code parses the content into `pid`, `hostname` and start token and hands them to `owner_is_stale`, whose docstring promises to return `True` "only when this process can prove the exact recorded owner is dead". That proof holds only if the owner wrote the record. A process of another account that can open the marker for writing uses `O_WRONLY | O_TRUNC` (no `O_CREAT`, so `fs.protected_regular` does not block it) and writes `2147483647
<host>

Its mtime and inode guard compares against what the contender read after the rewrite, so it passes. The contender, which runs as the marker's owner, does the rename, so the sticky bit allows it. On the next poll the contender's `O_EXCL` create succeeds. The first holder is not told: `SoftFileLock` has no heartbeat, and on release `_unlink_open_marker` finds another inode or no file at the path and returns without an error. The marker becomes writable by another account in two ways. An explicit `mode` with group or other write bits goes through `fchmod`, so the umask does not narrow it (`test_lock_mode_soft` at the scanned commit pins `-rw-rw-rw-` under umask `022`). With no `mode` argument, in a setgid and sticky group directory (`3770`), a second member of the group rewrote the marker and a second process of the holder's user acquired the same way. `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) run `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY` on a fresh connection for every acquire. That statement makes SQLite load the whole schema (the `sqlite_master` table, which lists every table and index with its `CREATE` text) of whatever file sits at the lock path. The caller's `timeout` reaches SQLite only as `busy_timeout`, which bounds waits for another connection's lock, not schema loading. The only content checks reject non-regular files and WAL mode (write-ahead log, an SQLite mode that keeps changes in a side file). A local user who can place or overwrite the file at a `ReadWriteLock`'s database path can therefore make every `acquire_read` / `acquire_write` of every process using that lock ignore its `timeout` and `blocking=False`. That position needs a non-sticky shared directory, or a database owned by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) that other users may write. A second 28 KB layout makes the acquire of a free lock run without end, spinning at 100% CPU and ignoring Ctrl-C. The effect is availability only: the other user reads nothing and corrupts nothing. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0. On the PR #834 head the `victim` process stops with a `ValueError` after 0.1 s at 24 MB peak RSS and the reproducer prints `OK`.  ## Impact  Another local user who can create or replace the lock database makes every `acquire_read` / `acquire_write` of every process using that `ReadWriteLock` run for a time of their choosing (about 500 bytes of disk per extra half second) while allocating about 1 GB, or not return at all, regardless of `timeout` or `blocking=False`. This goes beyond what holding the lock gives that user, because a held lock ends in `Timeout` when the caller's timeout runs out, and this does not. With the looping-page layout the acquiring thread spins at 100% of one CPU on a free lock, `Timeout` is not raised, Ctrl-C does not interrupt it, and only killing the process ends it. It is a denial of service of the lock user's process only: it reads nothing and corrupts nothing, and in the long-row case the lock is still granted afterwards.  ## Workarounds  - Keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. - Do not give the lock a database another account may write. The lock creates its database `0600`, and leaving it that way keeps other accounts from supplying its content. A lock shared between accounts through a `0666` database stays reachable even in `/tmp`. - If a stall or hang appears, the file at the lock path is the cause; replacing it with an empty file restores the lock.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. The stale-lock break shared by `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` (and their async variants, and a `FileLock` that has fallen back to a soft lock on `ENOSYS`, the "not implemented" error) recognises the marker it judged stale by two values. The marker is the lock file at `<path>`, whose presence says a process holds the lock. The values are its inode number (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) and its modification time (mtime) not being newer. The check runs after the contender has already closed the marker, so nothing keeps the inode allocated.  On a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight to the next file (ext4, xfs, overlayfs on them) the next holder's marker can carry that number. A contender still between its read and its break then renames and unlinks the live marker. Another local user (the other user below) who can create files in the lock's directory, a sticky `/tmp` included (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it), forces this at will. It plants a marker with a stale owner record and a modification time in the future and unlinks it as soon as a contender has read it. Two processes of the user running the lock (the lock user below) then hold the same default-configured lock at once, and nothing raises or logs. Affected versions: filelock >= 3.22.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-KIIS96IX`).  ## Severity  **CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N, 4.7 (Medium).**  `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): a race, though one the other user starts, lengthens (by making the lock user's `/proc` read slow) and retries at every release. The scanner measured 10 to 26 overlaps per 20-second run. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's processes act on their own. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user reads nothing. `I:H` (high integrity impact): two holders write the data the lock protects, and neither learns of the other. `A:N` (no availability impact): the lock keeps working.  Classification from the review: security, conditional on a sticky shared directory, ext4-style inode reuse and at least two contenders of the lock user. Our review verified it across UIDs (a UID is a user account's numeric id): the other user as uid 1001, the lock user's processes as uid 1000, BUG on 4.2.0 over ext4. The scanner rated it high (CWE-367).  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other user can create files in the lock's directory; a root-owned `1777` directory such as `/tmp` or `/var/tmp` is enough. It creates, `utime`s (sets the timestamps of) and unlinks only its own file. The sticky bit stops it removing the lock user's marker (checked: `EPERM`, operation not permitted), so the lock user's own stale break does the deletion. - The directory is on a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight to the next file. ext4 does (six create/unlink rounds returned one number six times, in the image's overlayfs `/tmp` and on a loop-mounted ext4), and xfs does. tmpfs returned six increasing numbers and the same run there gave no overlap, and btrfs does not hand a freed number back. - The lock user has at least two processes contending for the lock, and the displaced holder is still inside when the next contender polls (the breaker itself comes back one `poll_interval`, 50 ms by default, later). - The lock is `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock` or `SoftFileLease` (or async forms). The default `flock`-based `FileLock` joins them only after it has fallen back to `SoftFileLock` on `ENOSYS`. `StrictSoftFileLock` does not call `break_lock_file`, so it is not affected. - The same overlap also occurs with no other user involved, under heavy same-account contention, when a contender breaks a dead holder's marker and a successor creates its marker within the same timestamp tick (about once in 750 crashes with 64 workers on a 2-CPU machine, not on tmpfs).  filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit b831496, the re-check sits in [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L113-L118).
