### Summary  Pillow's libImaging `_decodeTile` decoder, used to decode tiled TIFF images, allocates a per-tile buffer using `realloc(state->buffer, TIFFTileSize(tiff))`. After each `TIFFReadTile` it then iterates `tile_y` from 0 up to `current_tile_length` and calls the configured row unpacker (here `copy4`) with the source pointer `state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size`. When libtiff returns a `tile_bytes_size` smaller than the worst-case `row_byte_size * tile_length`, the inner stride-and-copy loop walks past the realloc'd region and `copy4` performs a 1024-byte `memcpy` that reads up to `(tile_length-1) * row_byte_size + row_byte_size` bytes from a buffer sized only to `tile_bytes_size`. The supplied PoC TIFF triggers a 1024-byte over-read exactly 0 bytes past a 196608-byte allocation. An attacker who can convince a Pillow-using application to decode a crafted TIFF can trigger a process crash (DoS) and may cause adjacent heap memory to be copied into the decoded pixel buffer.  ### Details  Pillow's TIFF decoder, when libtiff reports the file is tiled, takes the `_decodeTile` path. The function:  1. Asks libtiff for `TIFFTileSize(tiff)` (the bytes-per-tile) and `TIFFTileRowSize(tiff)` (the bytes per row *as stored by libtiff*). 2. Reallocates `state->buffer` to exactly `tile_bytes_size`. 3. For each tile origin `(x, y)` and each plane, calls `TIFFReadTile` into `state->buffer`, then walks the tile row by row, calling the configured `ImagingShuffler` (here `copy4`) on each row's worth of source bytes.  The validation done before the loop is:  ```c if (tile_bytes_size > ((tile_length * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8) * tile_width) {     state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN;     return -1; } ```  This rejects oversized libtiff tiles, but it does **not** reject *undersized* ones — i.e. the case where libtiff returns a `tile_bytes_size` strictly **less** than `row_byte_size * tile_length`. The loop body, however, indexes into the buffer assuming the buffer is at least `row_byte_size * tile_length` bytes long.  ### Vulnerable Code  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:446-490 — _decodeTile new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes);   // bytes = tile_bytes_size if (!new_data) { ... } state->buffer = new_data;  for (y = state->yoff; y < state->ysize; y += tile_length) {     for (plane = 0; plane < planes; plane++) {         ImagingShuffler shuffler = unpackers[plane];         for (x = state->xoff; x < state->xsize; x += tile_width) {             if (TIFFReadTile(tiff, (tdata_t)state->buffer, x, y, 0, plane) == -1) { ... }              current_tile_width  = min((INT32)tile_width,  state->xsize - x);             current_tile_length = min((INT32)tile_length, state->ysize - y);             for (tile_y = 0; tile_y < current_tile_length; tile_y++) {                 shuffler(                     (UINT8 *)im->image[tile_y + y] + x * im->pixelsize,                     state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size,   // <-- OOB stride                     current_tile_width                 );             }         }     } } ```  ```c // src/libImaging/Unpack.c:1288-1291 — copy4 (the crash site) static void copy4(UINT8 *out, const UINT8 *in, int pixels) {     /* RGBA, CMYK quadruples */     memcpy(out, in, 4 * pixels);   // <-- ASAN-detected READ here } ```  The PoC's tile metadata yields `tile_width = tile_length = 256`, `row_byte_size = 1024` (4 bytes/pixel × 256 pixels), and `tile_bytes_size = 196608` (which is 256·256·3 = three-channel-byte storage). The realloc'd buffer is 196608 bytes. The unpacker iterates `tile_y` from 0 to 255 and for the highest rows the source pointer `state->buffer + tile_y * 1024` already lies at or past offset 196608 — the very last row's `memcpy(in=buffer+255·1024, 1024)` reads 1024 bytes starting `260096 - 196608 = 63488` bytes past the allocation; ASAN flags the very first byte past the heap region (`READ of size 1024 at … 0 bytes after 196608-byte region`).  The mismatch is real: libtiff's `TIFFTileSize` returns the *packed* per-tile storage (which depends on the file's photometric/separation layout — it can legitimately be smaller than `row_byte_size × tile_length`), while the inner loop strides as if the buffer always equals `row_byte_size × tile_length`.   ## Attribution  This issue was found by Anthropic from using Claude to study security of open source projects, and I am from Ada Logics helping validate the found issues and report to maintainers. The data in this report has been reviewed manually.

``` ============================================================================ OOB read in TiffDecode.c tile and RGBA paths leaks heap memory into pixels Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:483  in _decodeTile() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  Pillow reads past the end of a heap buffer when decoding certain malformed compressed TIFF files, and copies the bytes it reads into the pixels of the image it returns. An attacker who can get an application to open and load an image file, for example by uploading it to a service that returns thumbnails, previews or converted images, gets back fragments of that process's heap memory, including pointer values. A slightly larger file instead crashes the process. No special settings are needed, and nothing is written out of bounds.  The bug is in `_decodeTile()` and `_decodeAsRGBA()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. Both size their decode buffer from libtiff's view of the pixel layout (`TIFFTileSize()`/`TIFFTileRowSize()`, or `img.width * 4`). They then unpack each row with the unpacker that `TiffImagePlugin._setup()` chose from Pillow's own parse of the directory, and neither checks that the unpacker's input row fits inside the row libtiff produced. `_decodeStrip()` has exactly this check, added for OSS-Fuzz `crash-0da0` in 8.2.0, but the tile and RGBA paths never got it.  The two parsers can be made to disagree with a duplicated `PhotometricInterpretation` or `BitsPerSample` tag, because libtiff keeps the first occurrence and Pillow keeps the last. Pillow then unpacks 4 to 8 bytes per pixel from rows that libtiff filled with 1 to 4 bytes, so the last rows of each tile are read from beyond the buffer. The disclosed memory is a few tile rows past the buffer, and the attacker chooses the tile width. The amount does not grow with the number of tiles, because the buffer is reused for every tile.  The tile half was introduced in 1c295bf43 (first released in 8.2.0). The RGBA half was introduced in eb8c1206d, the CVE-2020-35654 fix (8.1.0).  The attached reproducer runs against an unmodified build. It writes three roughly 400-byte files that load without error, yet the last pixel rows of each change with glibc's malloc fill pattern and contain heap pointer bytes. A fourth file with a 65536x16 tile segfaults in `copy4` ← `_decodeTile` (`TiffDecode.c:483`) in most runs, depending on what is mapped after the buffer.  ## Details  `_decodeTile()` and `_decodeAsRGBA()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` size `state->buffer` from what libtiff says it will produce (`TIFFTileSize()`, resp. `img.width * 4`), but unpack each row with the shuffler that `TiffImagePlugin._setup()` selected from Pillow's *own* parse of the IFD. Nothing in either function checks that the unpacker's input row (`width * state->bits / 8` bytes) fits inside the row libtiff wrote. `_decodeStrip()` has exactly that check; the other two do not. Whenever the two IFD parsers disagree about the pixel layout — a tag with the wrong count or type that libtiff ignores but Pillow accepts, or a duplicated `PhotometricInterpretation`/`BitsPerSample`/`SamplesPerPixel` entry (libtiff keeps the first occurrence, `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` the last) — the unpacker reads past the end of the heap buffer and the bytes it reads become pixels of the returned image. Any Pillow rawmode wider than libtiff's actual sample layout works (`RGBX`, `RGB;16N`, `RGBA;16N`, `I;32`, `F;32F`, …); `RGBA;16N` (64 bits/pixel) against 1-bit libtiff data is the largest ratio, where every row after the first of each tile is read almost entirely from beyond the buffer.  The ~400-byte TIFF `tile_count2.tif` generated by the reproducer — one 16x16 tile, `BitsPerSample 8`, `SamplesPerPixel 1`, `Compression 8` (Adobe Deflate), and `PhotometricInterpretation` written as a SHORT with **count 2** (`6, 6`) — is opened by `Image.open()` as mode `RGB` with libtiff rawmode `RGBX`, and `load()` succeeds on the stock build. Rows 13–15 of the result contain bytes that lie 16, 32 and 48 bytes past the 256-byte tile buffer: decoding the same file twice under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=85` and `=170` yields identical rows 0–12 and different bytes in rows 13–15 (`aa` vs `55`, i.e. glibc's fill pattern). Under an ASan build of the extensions the same `load()` reports `heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 64` in `copy4` (`src/libImaging/Unpack.c:1290`) called from `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:483`, against the 256-byte region allocated at `TiffDecode.c:448`. The same layout with a single 65536x16 tile (4.5 KB file) makes the stock build SIGSEGV in `copy4 ← _decodeTile` reading an unmapped address in most runs (whether it faults depends on what is mapped after the 1 MiB buffer; a wider tile makes it reliable).  ### Why the two parsers disagree  libtiff 4.5 rejects a `PhotometricInterpretation` entry whose count is not 1 (`TIFFFetchNormalTag: Incorrect count for "PhotometricInterpretation"; tag ignored`), so for this file `TIFFGetField(tiff, TIFFTAG_PHOTOMETRIC, …)` returns 0 and libtiff treats the data as one 8-bit sample per pixel: `TIFFTileSize() = 256`, `TIFFTileRowSize() = 16`.  Pillow keeps the first value and carries on:  ```python # src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:762-770  (ImageFileDirectory_v2._setitem, reached from load())             try:                 (dest[tag],) = values             except ValueError:                 # We've got a builtin tag with 1 expected entry                 warnings.warn(f"Metadata Warning, tag {tag} had too many entries: ...")                 dest[tag] = values[0] ```  so `_setup()` sees `photo == 6`. `OPEN_INFO[(II, 6, (1,), 1, (8,), ())]` is `("L", "L")`, and because the file is compressed the libtiff branch then overrides the rawmode:  ```python # src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1578, 1600-1607         self.use_load_libtiff = READ_LIBTIFF or self._compression != "raw"         …             if photo == 6:                 self._mode = "RGB"                 if self._compression in "jpeg" and self._planar_configuration == 1:                     rawmode = "RGB"                 else:                     rawmode = "RGBX" ```  `RGBX` is a 32-bit rawmode, so `get_unpacker()` (`src/decode.c:301-309`) sets `state->bits = 32` and `state->shuffle = copy4`. The intent of the `photo == 6` override is that libtiff will deliver RGBA through `TIFFRGBAImage`, but that decision is made in C from *libtiff's* reading of the tag, which here is "not YCbCr":  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:737-764     TIFFGetField(tiff, TIFFTAG_PHOTOMETRIC, &photometric);   // unset -> stays 0     …     readAsRGBA = photometric == PHOTOMETRIC_YCBCR;          // 0     …         if (TIFFIsTiled(tiff)) {             _decodeTile(im, state, tiff, planes, unpackers); // unpackers[0] = copy4 ```  ### The missing check  `_decodeTile()` only guards against libtiff's tile being *larger* than what the unpacker expects, then allocates exactly `TIFFTileSize()` bytes and feeds `row_byte_size`-strided rows to the shuffler:  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:403-487  (_decodeTile)     tile_bytes_size = TIFFTileSize(tiff);                      // 256     …     row_byte_size = TIFFTileRowSize(tiff);                     // 16     …     if (tile_bytes_size > ((tile_length * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8) * tile_width) {         // 256 > 1024 is false -> no abort         …     }     state->bytes = tile_bytes_size;     new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes);           // 256-byte buffer (line 448)     …                 for (tile_y = 0; tile_y < current_tile_length; tile_y++) {                     shuffler(                                   // copy4: reads current_tile_width*4 = 64 bytes                         (UINT8 *)im->image[tile_y + y] + x * im->pixelsize,                         state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size, // from offset 16*tile_y                         current_tile_width                     ); ```  Row `tile_y` is read from `[16·tile_y, 16·tile_y + 64)`; for `tile_y` = 13, 14, 15 that ends 16, 32, 48 bytes past the 256-byte allocation. In general the last rows of every tile over-read by up to `(state->bits / libtiff_bits_per_pixel − 1) × row_byte_size` bytes, and `row_byte_size` scales with the attacker-chosen `TileWidth`.  Note also that the existing one-sided check at line 434 multiplies the file-controlled `tile_width`/`tile_length` (`UINT32`, accepted up to `INT_MAX` at line 428) by `state->bits` in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, so `tile_width * state->bits` wraps for `tile_width ≥ 2^32 / bits` (2^26 for the 64-bit rawmodes, 2^27 for `RGBX`/`I;32`/`F;32F`). An 8 KB file declaring a 2,097,152×1 image with `TILEWIDTH = 2^26+16`, `TILELENGTH = 1`, 1-bit data for libtiff and `RGBA;16N` for Pillow makes libtiff allocate an ~8 MB tile from which `unpackRGBA16L` reads 16 MB, and the stock build SIGSEGVs in `unpackRGBA16L ← _decodeTile (TiffDecode.c:483)`; a row-size comparison written in the same 32-bit arithmetic as line 434 would evaluate that row to 128 bytes and still accept it, so the new check must be done in a 64-bit type.  Compare the strip path, which refuses this situation (added for OSS-Fuzz `crash-0da0` in 8.2.0):  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:528-548  (_decodeStrip)     unpacker_row_byte_size = (state->xsize * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8;     …     row_byte_size = TIFFScanlineSize(tiff);     // if the unpacker calculated row size is > row byte size, (at least) the last     // row of the strip will have a read buffer overflow.     if (row_byte_size == 0 || unpacker_row_byte_size > row_byte_size) {         state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN;         return -1;     } ```  The identical file written with one strip instead of one tile fails `load()` with `OSError: decoder error -2` because of this check.  ### Same gap in `_decodeAsRGBA()`  `_decodeAsRGBA()` always produces `img.width * 4` bytes per row (`TiffDecode.c:325`, buffer allocated at line 339) and unpacks with `state->shuffle` (line 373) without looking at `state->bits`. It is reached when *libtiff* sees YCbCr while Pillow does not force `RGBX`. libtiff marks later duplicates of a tag as ignored (first occurrence wins); Pillow's `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` overwrites (`TiffImagePlugin.py:945`, last wins). The reproducer's `ycbcr_dup.tif` is a 16x16 Deflate strip with `PhotometricInterpretation` present twice (`6`, then `2`) and `BitsPerSample` twice (`8,8,8`, then `16,16,16`): libtiff decodes 8-bit YCbCr into a 1024-byte RGBA raster, Pillow selects `RGB;16N` (`state->bits = 48`), and `unpackRGB16L` reads 96 bytes per 64-byte row — ASan reports `heap-buffer-overflow` in `unpackRGB16L` (`Unpack.c:609`) from `TiffDecode.c:373`, past the 1024-byte region from `TiffDecode.c:339`.  The count-2 encoding is not the only lever, and on released versions it is not a lever at all: a 1-sample `photo == 6` file only gets rawmode `RGBX` since the unreleased commit 155330d63 ("Do not open YCbCr colorspace images as RGB without libtiff (#9779)", 2026-08-26). Released versions are reached through duplicated tags instead. A 3-sample tiled file with two `PhotometricInterpretation` entries (`1` or `2`, then `6`) produces the same `copy4` ← `_decodeTile` over-read, since libtiff keeps the first value and decodes 3 bytes per pixel while Pillow keeps `6` and unpacks 4 (the reproducer's `tile_dup.tif`). `ycbcr_dup.tif` above reaches `_decodeAsRGBA()` the same way.  ## Impact  Any application that calls `Image.open()` + `load()` (or `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `save()`, …) on an untrusted file reaches this with default settings: the file is content-sniffed as TIFF, and any compressed TIFF is decoded through libtiff and `TiffDecode.c` without `READ_LIBTIFF` being set. The over-read bytes are copied into the image's pixel rows, so a service that returns a thumbnail, preview or converted image hands adjacent heap memory back to the uploader, heap pointer values included — up to three libtiff tile rows past the buffer for the `RGBX`-over-8-bit case, with the tile row length (`TileWidth`) chosen by the attacker. `state->buffer` is allocated once and reused for every tile, so each tile re-reads the same region past that one buffer; the distinct heap disclosed per image is about `(unpacker_bpp / libtiff_bpp − 1)` tile rows and does not grow with the tile count. With a wide tile the read runs off the mapping and the process segfaults instead (the 65536x16 case crashes the stock build in most runs, depending on what is mapped after the buffer), taking down the whole worker rather than one request. Writes go to the correctly sized `Imaging` rows, so this is disclosure / crash, not memory corruption.  This is the same family as CVE-2020-35654 (Pillow and libtiff interpreting a YCbCr IFD differently in `TiffDecode.c`); that fix and the later `crash-0da0` fix closed the write and the strip-path read, but the tile path and the RGBA path still trust Pillow's rawmode over libtiff's row size. The tile-path gap was introduced in 1c295bf43c3a ("Check for dimensions and sizes to fit into int", 2021-01-25), which switched `_decodeTile()` from a buffer sized by Pillow's unpacker to `TIFFTileSize()`/`TIFFTileRowSize()`; it is first in Pillow 8.2.0. The `_decodeAsRGBA()` half dates from eb8c1206d6b1 ("Fix CVE-2020-35654 - OOB Write in TiffDecode.c"), first in 8.1.0.  ## Reproducing  Run `repro` (a single Python 3 script) against the installed, unmodified Pillow. No sanitizer build is needed. It writes four TIFFs into a temporary directory, decodes each one in a child process, and removes the directory at the end.  The script writes its TIFFs byte by byte with a small classic-TIFF writer. Each file has a single IFD and a single Deflate-compressed block. Deflate is only there so the file is decoded by libtiff and `TiffDecode.c`. Every pixel byte in the compressed data is defined, so the decoded image should not depend on anything else in the process:  - **`tile_count2.tif`**: a 16x16, 1-sample, 8-bit tile with `PhotometricInterpretation` written as SHORT count 2, `(6, 6)`. Pillow keeps `6` and unpacks with `copy4` (`RGBX`, 4 bytes per pixel). libtiff ignores the tag and decodes 1 byte per pixel. This lever needs 155330d63 (unreleased). - **`tile_dup.tif`**: a 16x16, 3-sample, 8-bit tile with `PhotometricInterpretation` present twice, `2` then `6`. libtiff keeps `2` (RGB, 3 bytes per pixel) and Pillow keeps `6` (`RGBX`, 4 bytes per pixel). This variant also applies to released versions. - **`ycbcr_dup.tif`**: the 16x16 strip with `BitsPerSample` `8,8,8` then `16,16,16` and `PhotometricInterpretation` `6` then `2`. libtiff decodes 8-bit YCbCr through `_decodeAsRGBA()` (4 bytes per pixel), and Pillow unpacks `RGB;16N` with `unpackRGB16L` (6 bytes per pixel). - **`tile_big.tif`**: the `tile_count2.tif` layout with a single 65536x16 tile.  For each of the first three files, the script runs `Image.open()` + `load()` + `tobytes()` twice, once with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=85` and once with `=170`. If the two outputs differ, bytes from beyond the decode buffer have become pixels. In that case it prints the first differing offset and the bytes around it from both runs. On this tree all three differ in their last rows: the `aa`/`55` fill bytes show up, along with heap pointer bytes. The script then decodes `tile_big.tif` and checks for a SIGSEGV (exit status -11). If `gdb` is available, it prints the top frames: `copy4` (`Unpack.c:1290`) ← `_decodeTile` (`TiffDecode.c:483`) ← `ImagingLibTiffDecode`. This crash depends on ASLR, so an occasional run may survive.  Each step prints which `_imaging` build it used and how Pillow opened the file (mode, size and rawmode). The script ends with a one-line summary. The last line is `BUG` if any file leaked heap bytes into its pixels or the big tile crashed the process. Otherwise it is `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch restores the `_decodeStrip()` invariant (the unpacker's input row must fit inside libtiff's row) in the two sibling decoders in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`, at the point where each one sizes its buffer:  - `_decodeTile()` computes `unpacker_row_byte_size = ((tsize_t)tile_width * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8` (the `tsize_t` cast keeps the product out of 32-bit arithmetic, so the `TILEWIDTH = 2^26+16` case above cannot wrap past the check on 64-bit builds). It reuses that value for the existing `TIFFTileSize()` sanity check, as `_decodeStrip()` does for strips. After that check and before the `realloc`, it fails with `IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN` when `unpacker_row_byte_size > row_byte_size` (`TIFFTileRowSize()`). - `_decodeAsRGBA()` fails with `IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN` when `state->bits > 32`, because `TIFFRGBAImage` rows are always 32 bits per pixel. This check runs before `TIFFRGBAImageBegin()` and any allocation.  With the patch, the tile and RGBA files fail `load()` with `OSError: decoder error -2`, the same result the equivalent strip file already gets. The patch also adds a regression test to `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` (`test_unpacker_row_wider_than_libtiff_row`). The test embeds the count-2 tile and the duplicated-tag YCbCr strip as base64, following the file's existing convention. The patch was applied to a clean tree and rebuilt: the reproducer no longer triggers, and `Tests/test_file_tiff.py`, `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` and `Tests/test_tiff_crashes.py` pass.  These checks close the over-read however the two parsers are made to disagree. Separately, `_setup()` could stop deriving the libtiff rawmode from tags that libtiff will read differently — e.g. treat a `PhotometricInterpretation`/`BitsPerSample`/`Compression` that is not a single well-typed value as "unknown pixel mode", the way `ImageWidth`/`ImageLength` are already required to be `int` at `TiffImagePlugin.py:1473`, or have `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` keep the first occurrence of a repeated tag as libtiff does (a behaviour change for malformed IFDs that is better made deliberately and separately) — but that only narrows the ways to reach the C-side gap rather than removing it: `TiffImagePlugin` cannot know how libtiff will resolve every malformed directory, and the decoder-side comparisons are what actually bound the read.  ## The patch  Reject TIFFs whose unpacker row is wider than libtiff's decoded row in _decodeTile() and _decodeAsRGBA(), as _decodeStrip() already does  Applies to `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` at the commit above.  ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py index 3d804ea4a..c08dfe77c 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py @@ -1232,6 +1232,50 @@ class TestFileLibTiff(LibTiffTestCase):              with pytest.raises(OSError, match="decoder error -9"):                  im.load()   +    @pytest.mark.parametrize( +        "data", +        ( +            # 16x16 8-bit greyscale tile, with a PhotometricInterpretation tag that +            # has two values. The size check runs only after Ghostscript has finished rendering and written the full raw image to a temporary file. An attacker who can upload a file of about 100 bytes makes each such request spend scale² times the Ghostscript rendering work and temporary disk space that the limit is meant to permit. For example, at scale 2 that is a 972 MB temporary file. The cause is in `Ghostscript()` in `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py`. It multiplies the file-declared size by the caller's `scale` (lines 93-94) and passes the product to `gs` as the `-g` output geometry. It never calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` on the scaled size. The only check is the one `Image.open()` ran on the unscaled size, so a file declaring 9000×9000 passes, and `load(scale=2)` then asks Ghostscript for 18000×18000 (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`). A file declaring 18000×18000 directly would be refused before Ghostscript ever ran. `DecompressionBombError` fires only when Pillow reopens the output file, so Pillow's own in-process allocation stays bounded and there is no memory corruption. The effect is a constant-factor overshoot rather than an unbounded one, for three reasons: * The multiplier is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file. * With the default warning filter, `Image.open()` already lets files up to 2× the limit reach Ghostscript at `scale=1`. * Any application feeding untrusted files to Ghostscript is already exposed to a tiny file that keeps Ghostscript busy indefinitely, since `gs` runs with no timeout. This is the EPS counterpart of the WMF `load(dpi)` gap closed in af70b075a. It has been present since the decompression-bomb limit was introduced in ce2955ec7 (2.5.0). The attached reproducer stubs out Ghostscript and shows a 76-byte file passing `Image.open()` and reaching `gs` with `-g18000x18000`. A one-line patch mirroring the WMF check is included. ## Details `EpsImageFile.load(scale=N)` (the documented way to rasterise an EPS at higher resolution) renders `width*N × height*N` pixels through Ghostscript, but the only decompression-bomb check on the way is the one `Image.open()` ran on the *unscaled*, file-declared `width × height`. The scaled product is never passed to `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` before `gs` is started. This 111-byte EPS declares 9000×9000 = 81,000,000 pixels, below the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (89,478,485), so `Image.open()` accepts it without even a warning: ``` %!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0 %%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000 %%EndComments 0 0 moveto 9000 9000 lineto stroke showpage ``` `im.load(scale=2)` on it then executes ``` gs -q -g18000x18000 -r144.000000x144.000000 -dBATCH -dNOPAUSE -dSAFER -sDEVICE=pnmraw -sOutputFile=/tmp/tmpXXXX -c 0 0 translate -f attack.eps -c showpage ``` i.e. asks Ghostscript for an 18000×18000 = 324,000,000-pixel raster (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`), whose `pnmraw` output is a 972,000,019-byte file in the temp directory. An EPS that declares 18000×18000 directly is rejected by `Image.open()` with `DecompressionBombError` before Ghostscript is ever run; via `scale=2` the same raster is rendered first and the `DecompressionBombError` only appears afterwards, when Pillow opens the file Ghostscript produced. The consequence is N² more Ghostscript CPU and temp-disk use per request than the configured limit intends; Pillow's own in-process pixel allocation remains bounded because `Image.open(outfile)` re-checks the PNM's size, and there is no memory corruption. ### Summary `PIL.EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript()` builds the Ghostscript command line using the input file path (`fp.name`) **without sanitization**, placing it at `-f <infile>`. A filename beginning with `-` is interpreted by Ghostscript as an option, giving command-line argument injection; chainable to RCE (see Impact). Reproduces with Pillow's default invocation (with `-dSAFER` enabled).  ### Details _Give all details on the vulnerability. Pointing to the incriminated source code is very helpful for the maintainer._  #### Type CWE-88 (Argument Injection) (→ CWE-78 (OS Command Injection) optionally, with attacker controlled text file)  #### Vulnerable Codes  ```python infile_temp = None if hasattr(fp, "name") and os.path.exists(fp.name):     infile = fp.name                      # user-controlled path used as-is, without validation else:     in_fd, infile_temp = tempfile.mkstemp()     os.close(in_fd)     infile = infile_temp     # ... (copy fp into a temporary file)  # Build Ghostscript command command = [     gs_binary,     "-q",     f"-g{width:d}x{height:d}",     f"-r{res_x:f}x{res_y:f}",     "-dBATCH",     "-dNOPAUSE",     "-dSAFER",                            # default sandbox — does NOT stop this injection     f"-sDEVICE={device}",     f"-sOutputFile={outfile}",     "-c",     f"{-bbox[0]} {-bbox[1]} translate",     "-f",     infile,                               # injected here: inserted into argv with no check for                                           # option prefixes (-, --) or Ghostscript's @-file token                                           # => argument injection (CWE-88)     "-c",     "showpage", ] # ... subprocess.check_call(command, startupinfo=startupinfo)   # spawns Ghostscript ```  #### Root cause.   When rendering an EPS image, PIL.EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript() constructs the Ghostscript command line using the input file path (fp.name) and places it directly at the -f <infile> position of the argument list. This path is user-controllable, yet Pillow performs no validation or neutralization of tokens that Ghostscript treats specially during command-line argument parsing — in particular a leading - or -- (which Ghostscript interprets as an option rather than a filename) and a leading @ (Ghostscript's argument-file syntax, which causes it to read additional command-line arguments from the named file). Because the filename is neither normalized (e.g., forced to an absolute path or prefixed with ./) nor checked against these prefixes before being handed to the subprocess, an attacker who controls the filename passed to Image.open() can inject arbitrary Ghostscript command-line arguments. This is a classic argument-injection flaw (CWE-88), and it is not mitigated by Pillow's default -dSAFER setting.  #### Affected - Pillow: tested on 12.3.0 (latest); vulnerable code is long-standing and appears to affect all current versions (main included). - Component: `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py`, `Ghostscript()` — `infile = fp.name`, and the command list entry `"-f", infile`.  #### Suggested fix Normalize the filename to an absolute path before it is passed to Ghostscript, so it can never be parsed as an option (`-`/`--`) or as an argument-file token (`@`): ```python     if hasattr(fp, "name") and os.path.exists(fp.name):         infile = os.path.abspath(fp.name)   # was: infile = fp.name ``` `os.path.abspath()` guarantees the path starts with a path separator (or a drive letter on Windows), so a leading `-` or `@` can no longer reach Ghostscript's argument parser. The `else` branch already builds a safe `tempfile.mkstemp()` path and needs no change.  ### PoC dockerfile, Default run shows the argument-injection demo (poc.py); for the RCE PoC run python3 poc-rce.py. ``` FROM ubuntu:24.04  RUN apt update RUN apt install -y --no-install-recommends python3 python3-venv ghostscript ca-certificates RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* RUN python3 -m venv /venv && /venv/bin/pip install --upgrade pip Pillow==12.3.0 ENV PATH=/venv/bin:$PATH WORKDIR /poc COPY poc.py . COPY poc-rce.py . COPY arg .  CMD ["python3", "poc.py"] ``` poc.py ``` import os from PIL import Image  ############################################################################################ # Attacker controlled file ############################################################################################  EPS = b"%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0
%%BoundingBox: 0 0 100 100
%%EndComments
showpage
"  name = "-h" with open(name, "wb") as f:     f.write(EPS)  ############################################################################################  print(f"[*] Pillow opens a file whose name is {name!r}") im = Image.open(name) print(f"[*] call `load()`; this paths calls `gs` command with '-f {name}'") try:     im.load() except Exception as e:     print(f"[*] load() raised: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")  print("CWE-88: argument injection; Pillow code doesn't validate argument name") print("        This poc.py shows the vulnerability clearly.") print("        If Pillow checks the name of file before it uses, It won't display `help`") ``` poc-rce.py ``` import os from PIL import Image  ############################################################################################ # Attacker controlled file ############################################################################################  EPS = b"%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0
%%BoundingBox: 0 0 100 100
%%EndComments
showpage
"  # To chain this vulnerability into critical RCE, We need another arbitrary text file # In this script, it is `arg`. name = "@arg" with open(name, "wb") as f:     f.write(EPS)  ############################################################################################  print(f"[*] Pillow opens a file whose name is {name!r}") im = Image.open(name) print(f"[*] call `load()`; this paths calls `gs` command with '-f {name}'") print(f"[*] and this leads to arbitrary command injection.") print(f"*********************************************") try:     im.load() except Exception as e:     print(f"*********************************************")     print(f"[*] load() raised: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")  print("") print("CWE-78: OS Command Injection;") print("CWE-88: Argument Injection  ; Pillow code doesn't validate argument name") print("        This poc.py shows the vulnerability clearly.") print("        If Pillow checks the name of file before it uses, It won't call `id`") ``` arg ``` -sOutputFile=%pipe%/bin/id -c 1 dict dup /OutputFile (%pipe%/bin/id) put setpagedevice ```  ### Impact **Confirmed — Ghostscript argument injection.** Because the filename is not validated, a leading `-`/`--` is parsed by Ghostscript as an option rather than a file. An attacker who controls the filename passed to `Image.open()` can therefore inject a Ghostscript command-line argument. Single-argument injection always succeeds.  **Potential RCE (verified).** The filename is also not validated against Ghostscript's `@`-file syntax: a filename of the form `@<path>` causes Ghostscript to read additional command-line arguments from `<path>`, allowing multiple arguments to be injected at once. If the attacker can additionally control the referenced file, this can be escalated to arbitrary command execution — an escalation we verified in our PoC (execution of `id`).  Applies under Pillow's default configuration (with `-dSAFER` enabled), on Pillow 12.3.0 with Ghostscript 10.02.1. With same GS arguments, I also confirmed RCE with latest GS version (10.07.1)  ### Why this is a Pillow bug (not the documented "block untrusted EPS" risk) This is not the malicious-EPS-content risk described in Pillow's security policy: the flaw is triggered by the filename, not by anything in the PostScript document. A completely benign EPS file still results in Ghostscript argument injection whenever the filename passed to Image.open() is attacker-influenced, so applications that legitimately process EPS remain affected — the guidance to block untrusted EPS input does not cover this. Because Pillow is the component that constructs the Ghostscript command line, ensuring a filename cannot be reinterpreted as an option (-/--) or an argument-file token (@) is Pillow's responsibility, not that of every downstream caller. The precondition — attacker influence over a filename that reaches Image.open() — is realistic (e.g., file-upload endpoints that preserve or derive the stored name from user input), and chaining it with this flaw yields RCE in practice, not just in theory. A one-line normalization (os.path.abspath(fp.name)) closes it without any change to how applications use the API.  ### Author Chanu Kang (from CysecLab at KAIST) @HLe4s

### Summary When text is drawn with a non-zero stroke width, Pillow creates a FreeType stroker and then loads each glyph. If `FT_Load_Glyph` fails for a glyph, the cleanup path calls `FT_Done_Glyph` on the `glyph` variable. That variable is not initialized before the first measurement loop, and in the render loop it is not reset to NULL after each glyph is freed. A malformed font loaded from untrusted bytes can force the load error and reach this free. This is a latent memory-safety defect; whether it crashes depends on the value in the uninitialized or stale pointer.  ### Details `glyph` is declared without a NULL initializer:  - `src/_imagingft.c:848`  The first measurement loop can jump to `glyph_error` before `glyph` is ever assigned:  - `src/_imagingft.c:1010-1013`  In the render loop the glyph is freed at the end of each iteration and not set back to NULL:  - `src/_imagingft.c:1242`  The cleanup frees it whenever a stroker exists:  - `src/_imagingft.c:1253-1256`  `ImageFont.truetype` accepts a file object or bytes, so the font is attacker-suppliable.  ### PoC This needs `fontTools` and any base TTF (the example uses one bundled with Pillow's tests). It rewrites glyph "A" to claim 5000 contours in a glyph body far too short for them, so `FT_Load_Glyph` returns an error while the face still opens.  ```python import struct from fontTools.ttLib import TTFont from PIL import Image, ImageFont, ImageDraw  SRC = "Tests/fonts/FreeMono.ttf"          # any TTF works as a base tt = TTFont(SRC) gid = tt.getGlyphID(tt.getBestCmap()[ord("A")]) loca_long = tt["head"].indexToLocFormat tt.close()  raw = bytearray(open(SRC, "rb").read()) nt = struct.unpack(">H", raw[4:6])[0] tbl = {} for i in range(nt):     rec = 12 + i * 16     tag = bytes(raw[rec:rec+4]).decode("latin-1")     off, length = struct.unpack(">II", raw[rec+8:rec+16])     tbl[tag] = (off, length) glyf_off = tbl["glyf"][0]; loca_off = tbl["loca"][0] if loca_long:     o0 = struct.unpack_from(">I", raw, loca_off + 4*gid)[0] else:     o0 = struct.unpack_from(">H", raw, loca_off + 2*gid)[0] * 2 struct.pack_into(">h", raw, glyf_off + o0, 5000)   # numberOfContours = 5000 open("evil.ttf", "wb").write(raw)  f = ImageFont.truetype("evil.ttf", 20)             # face opens d = ImageDraw.Draw(Image.new("RGB", (64, 64))) d.text((0, 0), "A", font=f, stroke_width=2)        # load error -> FT_Done_Glyph on bad pointer ```  Result on the pinned build: `FT_Load_Glyph` returns an error and execution reaches the `glyph_error` cleanup that calls `FT_Done_Glyph(glyph)` (the plugin surfaces `OSError: invalid outline`).  ### Impact Applications that draw text with `stroke_width != 0` using fonts loaded from untrusted bytes can hit an invalid or double free. The correct fix is small: initialize `glyph = NULL` and set it back to NULL after each `FT_Done_Glyph`.

On Pillow 12.3.0 and upstream `main` (`ad277e2761b489681e71b51e91367d46b0ceabb9`), a GIF with a long comment makes `_get_global_header()` copy portions of the comment repeatedly when saving, including comments carried over from untrusted images. I suggest provisional **Moderate** severity for crafted-image CPU denial of service, with CVSS-B 6.9 assuming a network service automatically opens unauthenticated uploads and they are resaved as GIFs; impact depends on input-size, concurrency, and worker CPU limits.

``` ============================================================================ Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF has 3+ IFDs Location: src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86 in MicImageFile.tell() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 5.6 KB image file makes Pillow loop forever at 100% CPU when an application asks how many frames the image has. This only affects installations that have the optional `olefile` package. Any application that opens an untrusted image and then reads `im.n_frames` can have one worker tied up indefinitely. That includes the common "is this image animated?" check and re-saving with `save_all=True` to TIFF, PDF or WebP. The call never returns, raises no exception, and does not grow memory, so only an external watchdog stops it. The file is a Microsoft Image Composer (MIC) container, which Pillow recognises by its magic bytes with no extension needed. Inside it is a TIFF stream with three chained image directories. `MicImageFile` subclasses `TiffImageFile` and overrides `seek()` and `tell()` so that a "frame" means one stream in the container. It still inherits `TiffImageFile.n_frames` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`), which walks the embedded TIFF's directory chain with `self._seek(self.tell() + 1)` until `_n_frames` is set. Two things stop that walk from making progress: - `MicImageFile.tell()` (`src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86`) returns the constant stream index. - `MicImageFile.seek()` calls `TiffImageFile._open()`, which resets `_n_frames` to `None`. As a result, the loop re-parses the second directory forever whenever the embedded stream has three or more directories. `Image.open()`, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. The regression was introduced in 0b33a87b0d15 (April 2020, first released in 7.2.0), which removed `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property. The attached reproducer builds the file in code and checks two controls, which return 3 and 1 frames as expected; the malicious file is still running when it is killed after 20 seconds. ## Details `MicImageFile` (registered for `Image.open` whenever `olefile` is installed) subclasses `TiffImageFile` and redefines a "frame" as one OLE `*.ACI/Image` stream, overriding `seek()` and `tell()` accordingly. It does not override the `n_frames` property, so the inherited TIFF implementation runs, and that implementation relies on `tell()` advancing as IFDs are loaded. `MicImageFile.tell()` returns the OLE stream index, which never changes inside `n_frames`, so the loop re-parses the same IFD forever. A 5632-byte OLE2 compound file whose `img0.ACI/Image` stream is a 351-byte TIFF with three chained 1×1 IFDs is enough. `Image.open()` on it succeeds (format `MIC`, detected by the OLE magic, no extension needed); evaluating `im.n_frames` then never returns and keeps one core at 100 %. A Python stack taken 27 s in is ``` File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1622 in _setup File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1271 in _seek File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1219 in n_frames ``` and instrumenting `_seek` shows it being called with `frame=1`, `tell()==0`, `_frame_pos==[8, 122]`, `_n_frames is None` on every iteration — identical state, so the loop is non-terminating, not merely slow. The same 351 TIFF bytes opened directly give `n_frames == 3` in milliseconds, and the same container around a 1-IFD TIFF gives `n_frames == 1`. The loop, `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`: ```python @property def n_frames(self) -> int: current_n_frames = self._n_frames if current_n_frames is None: current = self.tell() self._seek(len(self._frame_pos)) while self._n_frames is None: self._seek(self.tell() + 1) # 1219 self.seek(current) ``` and the overrides that break its progress assumption, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:76`: ```python def seek(self, frame: int) -> None: … self.fp = self.ole.openstream(filename) TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) # 82: resets _n_frames to None self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: return self.frame # 87: OLE stream index, not TIFF __frame ``` For a plain TIFF, `_seek(k)` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1236`) loads IFDs up to `k`, appending each offset to `_frame_pos`, setting `_n_frames` when an IFD's next-pointer is 0 (or already seen), and setting the private `__frame = k`; `TiffImageFile.tell()` returns `__frame`, so `self.tell() + 1` walks the chain to its end. For a MIC file, `Image.open` → `MicImageFile._open` sets `self._n_frames = len(self.images)` at line 69, but then calls `self.seek(0)` → `TiffImageFile._open` (line 82), which unconditionally sets `self._n_frames = None` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1203`) and `_seek(0)`s into the embedded stream. With the 3-IFD stream, IFD 0 has a non-zero next pointer, so `_n_frames` stays `None` after open. `n_frames` then runs: `current = self.tell()` is `0` (the OLE index); `_seek(len(_frame_pos))` = `_seek(1)` loads IFD 1, whose next pointer is also non-zero and not yet in `_frame_pos`, so `_n_frames` is still `None`. The `while` body computes `self.tell() + 1` = `0 + 1` and calls `_seek(1)` again; `len(_frame_pos)` is already 2, so nothing new is loaded — IFD 1 is re-read via `tag_v2.load` and `_setup()` and the state is unchanged. This repeats indefinitely; IFD 2 is never reached. Two chained IFDs are not enough (IFD 1's next pointer of 0 sets `_n_frames = 2` on the first `_seek(1)`); three or more are. `Tests/test_file_mic.py::test_n_frames` passes only because `hopper.mic`'s stream has a single IFD, so `_seek(0)` sets `_n_frames = 1` and the loop is never entered; the `len(self.images)` assignment at line 69 is only consumed by the initial `_seek_check(0)` and is overwritten before any caller can read `n_frames`. A side effect of the same mismatch: with a 2-IFD stream `n_frames` returns 2 (TIFF IFDs) while `seek(1)` indexes `self.images[1]` (OLE streams) and raises `IndexError` — visible with `save_all=True`. ## Impact Any application that lets Pillow open an uploaded file and then reads `im.n_frames` — the usual way to decide whether an image is animated (`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1) > 1`), and also what `hasattr(im, "n_frames")`/`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1)` in Pillow's own `TiffImagePlugin._save_all` (`:2333`), `PdfImagePlugin._save` (`:250`) and `WebPImagePlugin._save_all` (`:171`) evaluate when the app re-saves with `save_all=True` — can be made to spin one worker at 100 % CPU indefinitely with a 5.6 KB upload. The file needs no particular extension (OLE magic; `FpxImagePlugin` rejects it on CLSID and `MicImagePlugin` accepts it), default limits do not intervene, memory does not grow, and no exception is raised, so only an external watchdog ends it. Preconditions: `olefile` installed (it is an optional dependency; without it the MIC plugin is not registered) and the application touching `n_frames` or a `save_all` path. `Image.open()` itself, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. The regression was introduced in `0b33a87b0d15` ("Replaced property methods for n_frames and is_animated with normal properties", 2020-04-13), first released in 7.2.0, which replaced `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property with the `_n_frames` attribute that `TiffImageFile._open` overwrites. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that runs against the installed Pillow (with `olefile`, which is what registers the MIC plugin). It builds every input in code, writes each one to a temporary file named `x` with no extension (so Pillow identifies the format from its magic bytes), and opens it in a child Python process that runs `Image.open(path)` and prints `im.format` and `im.n_frames`. It builds two things in code: - `tiff(n)`: an `n`-page TIFF of 4×4 greyscale frames written by Pillow itself (`save_all=True`), so the IFDs are chained exactly as Pillow's own writer chains them. The last next-IFD pointer is 0. - `mic(stream)`: a minimal OLE2 compound file with a storage named `img0.ACI` that contains a stream named `Image`, which is the layout `MicImageFile._open` looks for. Sector 0 is the FAT and sector 1 is the directory. The stream starts at sector 2 and is padded to 4096 bytes, so the file doesn't need a mini-FAT. The result is 5632 bytes. It runs three inputs, each in its own child process with a hard 20-second kill: 1. control: the plain 3-page TIFF. Expected `TIFF n_frames = 3`. 2. control: a MIC wrapping a 1-page TIFF. Expected `MIC n_frames = 1`. 3. attack: the same MIC container wrapping the 3-page TIFF. The timeout is enforced by killing the child rather than by an in-process alarm, because a `TimeoutError` raised while `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` is parsing would be caught by its `except OSError` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:958`) and leave the IFD half-parsed instead of stopping the loop. The script prints `BUG` when both controls return and the attack child is still running after 20 seconds; otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, the attack case prints `MIC n_frames = 1` and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch restores the OLE-level frame count after the embedded TIFF stream has been opened, so the inherited `n_frames` never enters its IFD-walking loop and `n_frames`/`seek()` agree on what a frame is. In `MicImageFile.seek`, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:82`, right after `TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self)`: ```diff TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) + # TiffImageFile._open() resets the frame count to that of the + # embedded TIFF stream, but the frames of an MIC file are its streams + self._n_frames = len(self.images) + self.is_animated = self._n_frames > 1 + self.frame = frame ``` Doing this in `seek()` restores the invariant on every seek, not only the first. The existing assignments at lines 69–70 of `_open` are kept: the initial `seek(0)` → `_seek_check(0)` reads `n_frames` before `TiffImageFile._open` has run, so they are still needed. Plain read-only `n_frames`/`is_animated` properties, as before 0b33a87b0, are no longer a drop-in option because `TiffImageFile._seek` assigns `self.is_animated`. ``` ============================================================================ Quadratic GIF comment concatenation allows DoS in Image.open() Location: src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:266 in GifImageFile._seek() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Opening a crafted GIF file with `Image.open()` takes time that grows with the square of the file's size, so anyone who can submit an image to a service that uses Pillow can keep one worker busy at full processor load for a long time with a small file. A 2 MB file takes about 5 seconds to open, a 4 MB file about 35 seconds, and an 8 MB file about 3 minutes. An ordinary GIF of the same size opens in well under a second. The cost is paid inside `Image.open()` itself, with default settings, before the application has seen the image's size or format. The bug is in `GifImageFile._seek()` in `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py`, which builds `info["comment"]` by appending to an immutable `bytes` object with no size limit. It appends once per 255-byte sub-block (`comment += block`, line 261) and once per comment extension (`info["comment"] += b" " + comment`, line 266). Each append copies everything collected so far. A file made of many tiny comment extensions forces a full re-copy for each one. Because `_open()` ends with `self._seek(0)`, any code that only opens an uploaded file to identify it, read its dimensions, or make a thumbnail pays the full cost. The decompression-bomb check does not help, since the image is 1×1. Memory use stays linear, so the effect is processor exhaustion and latency, bounded by whatever upload size the service allows (about 1 second at 1 MB). This is the same kind of issue as the EPS open-phase slowdown fixed as CVE-2021-28677, here in the GIF comment handling. The quadratic pattern was introduced in commit b2b737b68b06 ("Allow arbitrary number of comment extension subblocks", November 2018) and has shipped since Pillow 5.4.0. The attached script builds 2 MB and 4 MB test files and compares each against a byte-identical control whose extensions are labelled as plain text instead of comment. The 4 MB comment file took about 34 seconds to open, against 0.26 seconds for its control. A patch that collects the pieces in a list and joins them once is also attached. ## Details `GifImageFile._seek()` collects GIF comment extensions into `info["comment"]` using `bytes` concatenation, once per 255-byte sub-block and once per comment extension, with no limit on the total. `bytes` is immutable, so every `+=` allocates a new object and copies everything accumulated so far; the work done by `Image.open()` is therefore quadratic in the amount of comment data in frame 0. A 1×1 GIF89a whose body is nothing but the 5-byte comment extension `21 FE 01 41 00` repeated makes this directly observable. `Image.open(BytesIO(data))` on such a file, stock build at this commit, 2-CPU machine: | file size | comment extensions (`21 FE …`) | same bytes labelled plain-text extension (`21 01 …`) | |---|---|---| | 1 MB | 1.2 s | 0.09 s | | 2 MB | 4.9 s | 0.13 s | | 4 MB | 35 s | 0.26 s | | 8 MB | 183 s | — | The control column is the identical byte stream with the extension label changed from `0xFE` to `0x01`; it goes through the same loop and the same `self.data()` reads but is discarded instead of concatenated, and scales linearly. No `load()` is needed and no warning or exception is raised; `im.info["comment"]` simply ends up holding the multi-megabyte blob. The code, `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:229-281` (trimmed): ```python elif s == b"!": s = self.fp.read(1) block = self.data() … elif s[0] == 254: # # comment extension # comment = b"" # Read this comment block while block: comment += block # :261 one copy per sub-block block = self.data() if "comment" in info: # If multiple comment blocks in frame, separate with info["comment"] += b" " + comment # :266 one copy per extension else: info["comment"] = comment s = b"" continue … while self.data(): # every other extension: read and drop pass ``` `self.data()` (`:97-102`) reads one length byte and then that many bytes, so each call is cheap and bounded; the cost is entirely in the two `+=` lines. For a single comment extension of N bytes delivered as N/255 sub-blocks, line 261 copies about N²/510 bytes in total (4 MB → 2.3 s, 8 MB → 9.5 s, 16 MB → 38 s measured). Splitting the same data into many small comment extensions is worse, because line 266 re-copies the whole of `info["comment"]` once per extension: with 1-byte extensions a file of F bytes causes roughly F²/25 bytes of copying, which is the table above (growth ×4–7 per doubling once the buffer outgrows the CPU caches). The simplest case is a `/Pages` root that lists itself as its own `/Parent`; a longer cycle among page-tree nodes behaves the same way. The loop performs no I/O and no allocation, so neither `MemoryError` nor the recursion limit intervenes. A longer cycle behaves identically as long as every node on it was reached through `linearize_page_tree()` and is therefore cached (e.g. root 2 → `/Kids [4 0 R]`, node 4 → `/Kids [3 0 R] /Parent 2 0 R`, and root 2 declaring `/Parent 4 0 R`); a `/Parent` pointing at an object that was never read raises `KeyError` instead, which is harmless. The parser already defends against exactly this shape of problem one level up: `read_prev_trailer()` (`src/PIL/PdfParser.py:699-722`) carries a `processed_offsets` list and raises `PdfFormatError("trailer loop found")` when a `/Prev` offset repeats — the fix for CVE-2026-42310. The `/Parent` walk in `rewrite_pages()` has no equivalent guard. The unguarded walk was introduced in `24ecfe315ab5` ("issue #2959: fix wrong Parent of pre-existing Page objects when appending", 2018-03-03) and has been in every release since 5.1.0. ## Impact Any application that appends pages to a PDF it did not produce — `im.save(fp, "PDF", append=True)` or `save_all=True, append=True` on a user-supplied document — hangs indefinitely with one CPU core pinned, on an input of a few hundred bytes. The loop is pure Python doing two dict lookups per iteration, so memory stays flat and memory limits do not end it; only an external watchdog does. In a web worker or batch converter that is a denial of service of that worker per request. The attacker needs to control only the bytes of the existing PDF; no non-default Pillow setting is involved beyond the application choosing the append path. Pillow does not open PDFs for reading, so plain `Image.open()` pipelines are not affected. This is a sibling of CVE-2026-42310 (infinite loop on a cyclic trailer `/Prev` chain in the same parser, same entry point): same class, different linked structure, and the guard added for that CVE does not cover it. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that runs against the installed Pillow (`/src/src/PIL`). Each has a Catalog (object 1), a `/Pages` root (object 2) and a `/Page` (object 3), and each has a correct xref table. The only difference between them is in object 2: - `control` has `<>`. ``` ============================================================================ APNG background disposal allocates full canvas before decompression bomb check Location: src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:1000  in PngImageFile._seek() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  A 126-byte animated PNG file makes Pillow's `Image.open()` allocate and fill memory sized by the image dimensions the file claims, before Pillow's built-in check for oversized images runs. A file claiming 22000×22000 pixels costs about 1.9 GB. Anyone who can get an application to open an image they supply, with default settings and no further calls such as `load()`, can cause a multi-gigabyte memory spike per file. If the claimed size exceeds the machine's free memory, the operating system kills the process outright.  The bug is in `PngImageFile._seek()` in `src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py` (around line 1000). For any APNG, `_open()` calls `self._seek(0)`. When the first `fcTL` chunk requests `OP_BACKGROUND` disposal, `_seek()` calls `Image.core.fill(self.mode, self.size)` with the full IHDR size, which allocates and zero-fills width×height×4 bytes. `OP_PREVIOUS` takes the same path, because frame 0 rewrites it to `OP_BACKGROUND`. This all happens inside the plugin factory, so `Image.open()`'s `_decompression_bomb_check(im.size)` only runs after the memory has been touched. A 1×1 frame rectangle passes the only checks on the way.  Below available memory, the allocation is freed when `DecompressionBombError` propagates, so sustained pressure needs repeated or concurrent uploads. A 45000×45000 header gets the process killed by the out-of-memory killer on an 8 GB host. The attached reproducer opens two such files that differ in one byte (`dispose_op` 0 vs 1). Both end in `DecompressionBombError`, but peak resident memory is 17 MB for the first and 1864 MB for the second. The eager fill was introduced in 5e4e0fa6ee67 ("Use disposal settings from previous frame", December 2020) and first shipped in 8.1.0. Two candidate patches with a regression test are attached.  ## Details  For an APNG whose first `fcTL` chunk requests `OP_BACKGROUND` disposal, `PngImageFile._open()` creates and zero-fills a core image of the full IHDR-declared size. This happens inside the plugin factory, i.e. before `Image.open()` gets to `_decompression_bomb_check(im.size)`, so the check that is meant to reject oversized headers without allocating anything runs only after the allocation has been made and touched.  The following 126-byte file (all chunk lengths and CRCs valid) makes `Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))`, with default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` and no `load()`, reach 1.86 GB resident (`ru_maxrss`) and then raise `DecompressionBombError`. The byte-identical file with `dispose_op=0` raises the same error at 17 MB.  ``` IHDR  width=22000 height=22000 bit_depth=8 colour_type=6 (RGBA) acTL  num_frames=2 num_plays=0 fcTL  seq=0 w=1 h=1 x=0 y=0 delay=1/10 dispose_op=1 (OP_BACKGROUND) blend_op=0 IDAT  zlib(00 00 00 00 00)                      # one 1x1 RGBA scanline IEND ```  With `width=height=45000` (8.1 GB canvas) the same call attempts the full allocation: under a 4 GiB `RLIMIT_AS` it fails with `MemoryError` from the allocator instead of `DecompressionBombError`; without a cap, on an 8 GB host with no swap, the process is OOM-killed.  ### Code path  `Image.open()` runs the bomb check only after the plugin's constructor (and therefore `_open()`) has returned:  ```python # src/PIL/Image.py:3699-3701                     im = factory(fp, filename)                     _decompression_bomb_check(im.size)                     return im ```  For a plain PNG that ordering is fine: `PngImageFile._open()` only parses chunks up to the first `IDAT` and records `self._size` from `IHDR`; nothing is allocated from it. For an APNG (`acTL` seen, so `im_n_frames` is set) `_open()` additionally positions on frame 0:  ```python # src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:845-853         if self.png.im_n_frames is not None:             …             self._seek(0) ```  `_seek(0)` copies `disposal` and `bbox` from the `fcTL` chunk into `self.dispose_op` / `self.dispose_extent` and then prepares the disposal image for the *next* frame eagerly, using the full image size:  ```python # src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:991-1001         if self._prev_im is None and self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_PREVIOUS:             self.dispose_op = Disposal.OP_BACKGROUND          self.dispose = None         if self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_PREVIOUS:             …         elif self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_BACKGROUND:             self.dispose = Image.core.fill(self.mode, self.size)             self.dispose = self._crop(self.dispose, self.dispose_extent) ```  `Image.core.fill` is `_fill()` in `src/_imaging.c:711`, which does `ImagingNewDirty(mode, xsize, ysize)` followed by `ImagingFill()`; `ImagingFill` (`src/libImaging/Fill.c:23`) writes every row, so the whole `width*height*4` bytes become resident rather than merely reserved. `self.size` here is the IHDR size (22000×22000), not the 1×1 frame rectangle. The `_crop` on the next line does call `_decompression_bomb_check`, but on the `fcTL` rectangle (1×1) and only after the fill has completed. Lines 991-992 rewrite `OP_PREVIOUS` to `OP_BACKGROUND` on frame 0, so `dispose_op=2` takes the same path (verified: identical 1.86 GB peak). When the first `fcTL` rectangle is large, the `_crop` copy is a second extent-sized buffer on top of the full-canvas fill, so the transient peak can reach about twice the canvas: a 13000×13000 full-frame `fcTL` (below the error threshold, so `Image.open()` succeeds with only a `DecompressionBombWarning`) peaks at 1.31 GB for a 0.66 GB canvas.  The only validation `chunk_fcTL` applies (`src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:740-745`) is that the frame rectangle fits inside the IHDR size, which a 1×1 frame always does; IHDR width/height themselves are unconstrained 32-bit values at this point. Control then returns to `_open_core`, `_decompression_bomb_check((22000, 22000))` raises, and the 1.9 GB core image is released when the half-constructed `PngImageFile` is discarded.  The eager full-size fill in `_seek()` was introduced in `5e4e0fa6ee67` ("Use disposal settings from previous frame", 2020-12-24) and first shipped in 8.1.0; before it, the `OP_BACKGROUND` fill lived in `load_end()` and could not be reached from `Image.open()`.  ## Impact  Any application that calls `Image.open()` on untrusted bytes with default settings — the configuration in which the decompression-bomb check is supposed to make that call cheap and safe — can be made to allocate and write an attacker-chosen amount of memory from a ~126-byte PNG upload, before any error is reported and without `load()`, frame iteration, or `LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES`. The amount is set directly by the IHDR width/height (4 bytes per pixel for colour type 6): values below the host's free memory cause a transient multi-GB spike per request (≈15,000,000× amplification at 22000×22000) that is freed when the exception propagates, so concurrent or repeated uploads are needed to sustain pressure; values above it get the worker process OOM-killed outright. PNG is accepted by essentially every upload pipeline, and the file passes `_accept` and chunk CRC checks as a well-formed APNG.  This is the same class as the recent bomb-check additions for WMF (load at a different DPI), FITS, GIF and FontFile — an allocation sized from file-declared numbers on a path `_decompression_bomb_check` does not cover — but here the uncovered path is `Image.open()` itself rather than a later `load()`/`seek()`.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script (no build step, no companion files). It builds two PNGs in memory, opens each one with plain `Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))` in a fresh child interpreter using default settings and no `load()`, and has each child report the exception it got and its own peak RSS (`ru_maxrss`). It needs about 2 GB of free RAM and finishes in about a second.  The two files are 126 bytes each and differ in exactly one byte, the `dispose_op` of the first `fcTL` chunk: `0` (`OP_NONE`) for the control and `1` (`OP_BACKGROUND`) for the attack. Both declare IHDR 22000×22000 RGBA. That is 484 Mpixel, above the 2×`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` error threshold, so `Image.open()` has to reject both with `DecompressionBombError`. Each chunk has a job:  - The `acTL` chunk (2 frames) makes `_open()` call `_seek(0)`. - The 1×1 `fcTL` rectangle passes `chunk_fcTL`'s bounds check and `_crop`'s bomb check. - The one-scanline `IDAT` ends header parsing.  Expected output on this tree:  ``` 126-byte APNG declaring 22000x22000 RGBA; Image.open(BytesIO(data)), defaults   control  dispose_op=0 OP_NONE        -> DecompressionBombError peak RSS    17 MB   attack   dispose_op=1 OP_BACKGROUND  -> DecompressionBombError peak RSS  1864 MB Image.open() touched a full 22000x22000 canvas before the bomb check ran BUG ```  Both files are rejected, but the control is rejected at interpreter size. The attack file only reaches the bomb check after `Image.core.fill("RGBA", (22000, 22000))` has allocated and zero-filled about 1.9 GB. The script prints `BUG` if the attack child's peak RSS is at least 1000 MB and at least 20× the control's, or if the attack child is killed by `SIGKILL` (for example by the OOM killer on a small host). Otherwise it prints `OK`; any other non-zero child exit is treated as a harness failure, printed with the child's output, and also ends in `OK`. With either attached patch applied, both children report about 17–22 MB and the script prints `OK`.  The allocation grows with the header, so it can be scaled by changing `SIZE` in the script. The 45000×45000 case (an 8.1 GB canvas) is covered in Details and is not part of the script.  ## Suggested fix  Do not build the `OP_BACKGROUND` disposal image from the declared size during `_open()`. ### Summary The MSP RLE decoder expands run-length data into an in-memory buffer with no cap tied to the declared image size. A small file that passes the pixel-count check can force hundreds of megabytes or more of allocation when the application loads pixels.  ### Details The MSP decoder writes each run into an unbounded `io.BytesIO` and can expand roughly 85x per run:  - `src/PIL/MspImagePlugin.py:144-146`  ### Impact Memory-exhaustion denial of service from a tiny crafted image in any application that loads pixels. The expansion is decoupled from the declared pixel count, so `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` does not bound it.

``` ============================================================================ Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:94  in _tiffWriteProc() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  Pillow can write attacker-chosen data past the end of a heap buffer when it saves a TIFF image to an in-memory destination such as `io.BytesIO` rather than to a file. The same code also copies leftover heap memory from the process into the saved file. Anyone who can supply an image to a service that opens it and re-saves it as TIFF this way can trigger this with default settings. The attached reproducer crashes the process, and the overflow could potentially be developed further, but code execution is not demonstrated here.  The bug is in `_tiffWriteProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. This is the write callback for the in-memory sink that Pillow gives libtiff whenever the save target has no `fileno()`. While writing the directory, libtiff seeks past the current end of data and writes tag values there. `_tiffWriteProc` sizes its `realloc()` from `state->size + size` instead of from the write position `state->loc`. As a result, the first out-of-line tag value written after that seek can run past the allocation by up to the size of the directory: 12 bytes per entry, 126 bytes in the minimal case, and 2384 bytes observed with a 331-entry directory. The overflowing bytes are the tail of a tag value taken from the uploaded file.  No save options are needed, because compression and tags are inherited from the source image. The overflow does require an attacker-sized out-of-line tag to reach libtiff. That happens when the opened TIFF is saved directly (ImageDescription, DocumentName or XMP), or through an embedded ICC profile, which survives `copy()` in `im.info`. The bytes libtiff skips for alignment are never initialised, so any compressed TIFF over 64 KiB written this way also leaks one stale heap byte per padding hole. That leak needs no crafted tag.  The attached reproducer builds a 131 KB PackBits TIFF and runs `Image.open(...).save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")`. Saving the same image to a file path succeeds, but the `BytesIO` save aborts with glibc's `malloc(): corrupted top size`. A second part of the script shows uninitialised heap bytes at the padding offsets of a `BytesIO` save that are zero in the file save. Saves to real files are unaffected. The defect dates to e782fe721e01 (2013) and has been present since Pillow 2.0.0.  ## Details  When `im.save()` writes a TIFF through libtiff to a target that has no usable `fileno()` (`io.BytesIO`, an HTTP response object, a storage backend stream), libtiff is opened with `TIFFClientOpen()` on Pillow's own in-memory sink, `_tiffWriteProc` / `_tiffSeekProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. libtiff treats that sink like a file: when it writes the directory it seeks *beyond* the current end of data (to `eof + IFD size`, where the out-of-line tag values go, and one byte further after every odd-length tag value to keep offsets even) and writes there. On a real file the kernel grows the file and zero-fills the gap. The memory sink does neither correctly:  1. `_tiffWriteProc` sizes its `realloc()` from `state->size + size` instead of `state->loc + size`, so the first write after such a seek can land past the end of the new allocation — a heap buffer overflow whose content is tag data taken from the image being saved. 2. The bytes that libtiff skips are never written, and the grown region is a bare `realloc()`, so they reach the output TIFF with whatever the heap held before.  Both are reachable with default settings by the ordinary "re-encode the upload" sequence `Image.open(upload); im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")` with no save options: `compression` defaults to the source file's (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1734`), any compression other than raw selects the libtiff writer (`:1746`), the source's `tag_v2` entries are passed through to libtiff (`:1959`), and a target without `fileno()` leaves `_fp = 0` (`:1928-1935`), i.e. the memory sink. The overflow half additionally needs an attacker-controlled out-of-line tag value of the right length to reach libtiff. With the opened `TiffImageFile` saved directly (`tag_v2` passthrough) that can be a ~64 KiB ASCII tag (269/270/271/272) or the XMP packet (tag 700, type BYTE — arbitrary bytes), and the number of tags the upload carries sets the IFD size, i.e. the overrun length (12 bytes per entry; 2384 bytes with a 331-entry IFD observed). After `convert()`/`resize()`/`thumbnail()`/`copy()` the `tag_v2` entries are gone, but `im.info["compression"]` (still selecting libtiff) and `im.info["icc_profile"]` survive and the ICC profile is written as tag 34675 (`:1822-1824`), an equally attacker-controlled out-of-line value: `Image.open(x).copy().save(BytesIO(), "TIFF")` with the payload in the ICC profile produces the identical ASan report. The stale-byte half needs no attacker tag at all.  **Proof (overflow).** A 131 198-byte hand-built TIFF — mode L, 7×8191, `Compression=32773` (PackBits), an `ImageDescription` of 65 535 characters — opened with `Image.open()` and saved with `im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")` aborts a stock build with glibc's `malloc(): corrupted top size`. The same call against an AddressSanitizer build of the C extensions reports  ``` AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow ... WRITE of size 65536  #1 _tiffWriteProc src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:115  #4 TIFFFlush  #5 ImagingLibTiffEncode src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1056 0 bytes to the right of 131072-byte region, allocated by realloc in _tiffWriteProc src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:103 ```  **Proof (uninitialised bytes).** Saving one 300×300 RGB image as `compression="tiff_lzw"` with four odd-length ASCII tags to a `BytesIO`, once with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=1` (glibc fills fresh allocations with 0xfe) and once with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` (0x55), gives two 369 463-byte TIFFs that differ in exactly 4 bytes, 0xfe vs 0x55, at offsets 369177, 369417, 369423, 369451 — the pad byte between the odd-length last strip and the IFD, and the pad byte after each odd-length tag value except the last. Without any allocator tweaks, after a few 64 KB–400 KB Python `bytes` objects filled with 0xa7 are created and freed, re-saving an uploaded LZW TIFF carrying ten odd-length ASCII tags yields 0xa7 at all nine pad offsets.  ### Code walk-through  The sink's state is `{data, size (allocated), loc (position), eof (high-water mark)}`; the encoder path starts it as a zeroed 64 KiB block (`TiffDecode.c:863`, `calloc(bufsize, 1)` with `bufsize = 64*1024`, `flrealloc = 1`).
